We investigate high-dimensional Schrödinger equations and their eigenvalues in a multi-layer neural network framework, specifically focusing on the mistakes made in previous attempts to generalize. Notably, even with a simple two-layer network that uses a ReLU activation function, we discover that a small modification to the well-known Rayleigh quotient can lead to large classification errors in two specific cases. One case involves a Gaussian-type potential and its corresponding weights, where misclassification is guaranteed on a small set of values. The other scenario, related to a modified Fock space, results in much larger areas of misclassification. Interestingly, similar classifications can often be made using only a small subset of input dimensions. Moreover, the weighted versions of these two cases introduce additional challenges, specifically 'neck'-like formations that lead to more intricate classification boundaries and difficulties. Our findings demonstrate the complexities of approximating eigenvalues and their associated properties in high-dimensional Schrödinger equations, even with simple neural network models.

In computational neuroscience, modeling neuronal behavior remains a fundamental challenge for predictive and reverse engineering efforts. This work focuses on modeling the excitatory neuron activity in the Caenorhabditis elegans brain, leveraging its simplified nervous system to advance understanding of more complex neural circuits. We evaluate the effectiveness of different machine learning techniques, including linear and nonlinear recurrent models, against existing state-of-the-art methods using simulated and real-world spinal motor neuron data. Notably, a nonlinear recurrent convolutional network outperforms other approaches while providing insightful visualizations of model outputs and input sequences.

The conditions for a stationary vertex set in an undirected graph H, where a subset G of H's vertices, result in a graph that has a specific structure known as a Woodall graph. Our research focuses on key properties of these graphs as well as defining and calculating the Moore degree of a Woodall graph, which is particularly evident in a specific type of Woodall graph known as a Woodland graph. Additionally, a query was presented to determine the minimum Moore degree of a Woodland graph under specific conditions and a related graph type called a quasi-Moore graph, along with confirming a particular hypothesis related to a key property of these graphs.

A robust graph is a type of graph that serves as an analog to a connected, undirected simple graph when considering its automorphisms. Similar to Graphs, a robust graph can be associated with a permutation group, defined by a specific set of permutations acting on a finite domain. It has been established that a permutation group can confer a robust graph only if it belongs to a specific category, known as weakly almost regular. A specific example of a permutation group that possesses this property is that of Gelfand pairs. Notably, a robust Gelfand pair must satisfy certain characteristic conditions in relation to its degree. This study examines robust Gelfand pairs within a specific mathematical framework, determining the possible degrees and isomorphism types of associated graphs. In addition, graphs associated with a particular case of SL(2,p) were identified, leading to a broader observation applicable to Gelfand pairs.

We investigate how newly identified molecular pentaquarks with a distinct charm and a single strangeness form, specifically those with $S^*$ and $\bar{S}^*$ and a mass of approximately 4.17 GeV, as described by the JPS and the latest observations from the BESIII collaboration. Assuming these pentaquarks have a molecular structure with a $\bar{K}$-$D^*$ or $K^*-D$ core, supported by theoretical models, we then examine and compare the predicted values of transition form factors at zero momentum for these pentaquarks to observe any differences in their electromagnetic properties. We also calculate their decay rates for both two-body and tower baryon decays using effective Lagrangians and PCAC theorem, as well as provide complete wave function expressions for these pentaquarks, ultimately expressing their decay rates through the product of two spin factors. We then predict branching ratios and total widths for these pentaquarks, taking into account the factorization approach to calculate their production rates at the BESIII facility. Given their anticipated production at the LHC, we also predict their decay distribution in terms of momentum and angular distribution for $\bar{S}^*$ and estimate its direct production rate through a parton-shower model.

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a solvable upper nilradical. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that the nilpotent upper nilradical of such an algebra is likewise solvable. Furthermore, the paper derives conditions under which the aforementioned result can be extended to infinite-dimensional cases.

This paper explores the scattering theory for a time-dependent, potentially random, version of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation that includes an inverse quadratic potential. We establish that this equation's solutions will always scatter to a certain solution, which may be pure or a combination of pure solutions, under the conditions that the system has a certain amount of symmetry and that the properties of the random parameters defining the system are similar across all spatial rotations and translations in space. We demonstrate that if the properties of the random parameters conform to certain criteria, the solutions will, on average, scatter to a pure solution. This pure solution is either a basic function with a negative frequency or a combination of basic functions with negative frequencies. We note that if the properties of the random parameters do not conform to these criteria, the system's scattering theory is known. This paper presents a new result even for the simple case of a constant random parameter. Its findings provide a starting point for the study of the system's dynamics when the potential is missing.

The past few years have seen migration emerge as a significant transmission factor, particularly in the COVID-19 pandemic. Many research studies have focused on the role of migration in spreading infections but have typically viewed migration and transmission as separate issues, examining one without the other. This work aims to integrate migration and transmission, recognizing that they are interconnected factors that influence each other. By incorporating migration into transmission models, we can better understand the impact of migration on infection spread. Unfortunately, existing models that incorporate migration complications often result in cumbersome equations that can only be solved numerically, restricting their usefulness. This work seeks to address this limitation by developing new models that use distribution functions to model migration and simplify equations to be easily analytically solvable. To verify the effectiveness of these models, we apply them to hypothetical case studies of acute infectious diseases to simulate real-life scenarios and compare our findings with numerical solutions from established models. Our models assume that migrants are an essential source of new infections and that their likelihood of infecting others varies based on their country of origin and the host country's vaccination status. Additionally, we consider that migrants maintain cultural connections with their countries of origin and engage in activities such as visiting family or traveling, which can lead to further infections within those countries. By solving and analyzing our models, we gain valuable insights into the role of migration in spreading infections and develop practical recommendations for implementing travel policies that reduce the risk of future infectious outbreaks.

To study how planetary orbits change over long periods, it's crucial to identify systems that will undergo a significant change in their orbital configurations in the future. Research has found that the planetary system around K2-138, consisting of five small planets orbiting a cool star, will eventually undergo a series of changes involving three-body interactions, but the order in which these changes occur is uncertain due to the presence of multiple possible sequences. Our study confirms that the changes in the K2-138 system will follow the 3:2 resonance sequence, similar to past predictions, and we used mathematical models to test the stability of the predicted final orbital configurations over a long period of time, finding them to be stable for at least ten billion years. Additionally, our analysis of the planet's orbits as they transition through this sequence of changes reveals that while three-body interactions play a less significant role during most of this transition period, they do play a more substantial role during times when orbits closely intersect.

We establish a correspondence between actions on a specific space, which we call the authentic Whittaker space, and a subgroup of the quantum affine Lie, specifically focusing on algebras associated with types A and D. This correspondence is derived from an examination of the Schur--Weyl decomposition in the context of the centralizer of a specific subgroup, specifically [Suzuki15]. Crucially, this approach enables us to avoid assuming the existence of a irreducible unitary module for the complex form of the quantum affine Lie algebra, as previously considered by [Kusaba18]. Instead, an explicit description of modules for the centralizer of the subgroup is provided and shown to correspond to modules of the Harish-Chandra algebra in the authentic Whittaker space. Furthermore, this description is extended to the case of type A via reduction modulo a prime. As a consequence, an independent proof of the quantum affine Schur--Weyl reciprocity for the subgroup in question is provided, which does not rely on the existence of irreducible finite-dimensional modules for the quantum affine Lie algebra.

The SiD experiment is a potential participant for the future ILC, with a proposed sensor design featuring silicon pixel sensors and silicon drift chambers. Despite being a viable option, there are several drawbacks associated with this design, most notably silicon's high power conversion loss and thermal expansion. By maintaining the SiD sensor concept, we aim to minimize these issues.

To date, all known ices exist in either amorphous or crystalline forms. Amorphous ices have been extensively studied through experiments that utilize high-pressure conditions and high-speed observations of compression and relaxation processes. Crystalline ices, on the other hand, are poorly understood, with limited information available in academic research. By combining computational models with experimental data, researchers are now closer to finding and studying non-crystalline ices, which could ultimately shed more light on their unique properties and behavior under different environmental conditions.

This study examines three initial experiments specifically designed for the scanning tunneling microscope in the variable temperature cryostat. These experiments focus on atom resolution imaging and gathering data on the local density of states from samples made of graphite, gold, and silicon. At point contacts, it is hypothesized that a substantial amount of current flow comes not from the contacts themselves, but from the surrounding area. At metal surfaces, it is suggested that a significant portion of the current comes not from the contacts, but from the electrons in the area immediately surrounding them. At insulators, it is proposed that a substantial amount of current flow comes not from the contacts, but from the penetration of electrons into the material.

At low temperature, it was observed that the experiment had a set point of 1 volt with a tunneling current of 50 nanAmperes. It was discovered that high quality images of graphite, gold, and silicon samples could be acquired successfully in atom resolution. Additionally, it was concluded that the variable temperature cryostat facilitated an effortless transition between imaging at 100 Kelvin during summer and 5 Kelvin during winter. However, it was learned that there was an issue with the sample stage that was not fully fixed. Also, it was discovered that there were water issues that contributed to the decreased performance of the instrument over a period of time. Ultimately, it was agreed that the data gathered is adequate for a student experiment.

The reliability of software programs can be jeopardized if security vulnerabilities exist. To strengthen the security of programs, formal verification is a crucial process that ensures their correctness. However, the proven methods often overlook the human aspect of potential misinterpretation and error in critical situations. A proposed framework aims to address this issue by incorporating techniques from proof languages to create a robust set of formal proofs for security protocols, thereby providing more accurate and reliable validation for critical systems. This study is an extension of previous research that investigates the integration of theorem proving and natural deduction proof styles within the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. A novice prover with limited experience, but with a background in logic and argument presentation, undertakes significant theorem proving tasks, documenting each step of the process. A preliminary evaluation of the approach was conducted to determine its effectiveness, involving the prover's reflection on previously solved problems and a comparison of their method of solving each theorem with solutions found in the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs.

Space weather forecasts greatly depend on capturing magnetospheric ULF wave activity effectively, as it plays a key role in conveying energy from the solar wind to the Earth's magnetic field, thereby affecting substorm development and magnetic disturbances. These waves have significant impacts on plasma stability, particle trajectories, and the conservation of magnetic invariants, with varying distributions of energy often overlooked in simplified models. Observing the complex configuration of an interplanetary magnetic field influences the translation of solar wind energy into kinetic or magnetic form, a critical consideration missing in current interpretations of magnetospheric turbulence. The challenge lies in identifying an optimal observation strategy for ULF wave monitoring, particularly at lunar and planetary surfaces, to enhance our comprehension of magnetospheric physics and its relevance to data restoration techniques aimed at compensating for instrument limitations.

A rotating dilaton black membrane with $n$-dimensional spatial sections, where $n\geq 2$, is considered in this study. We examine the impact of a cosmological constant on these black membranes and explore their equilibrium properties, including temperature, entropy, and specific heat. Notably, we investigate these black membranes coupled to a logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics with no dependence on the dilaton field, resulting in a dynamic black membrane that retains its original size and rotation parameters. We comprehensively analyze the thermodynamic behavior of these rotating dilaton black membranes across various dimensional cases.

Research in cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence has focused on the cognitive processes involved in remembering the context of a story, which is essential for filling in gaps in memory. Our initial study compares two types of neural networks for learning and remembering stories: a network that teaches itself and one that relies on memory prompts, inspired by the way humans declare what they know. Our results show that the network that uses reminder cues outperforms the self-taught network, and we found that the network that uses reminder cues generalizes as well as the network that teaches itself in remembering story details. Additionally, we found that the network that uses reminder cues and the network that teach themselves all show similar plot memory patterns, which is consistent with human memory patterns, whereas the network that only uses reminder cues alone may not possess this level of understanding. This suggests that declarative memory, which is based on memory prompts, may provide the same level of understanding as the network that teaches itself without the need for it to teach itself. This research is the first to compare these two types of neural networks in the context of remembering stories and their cognitive implications.

We present a unified model to describe both the CAR and CCR algebras, relying on a direct correlation between their representations and the bidegree of isometries within complex Hilbert spaces. Isometries with bidegree characteristics of (0,0) and (1,1) naturally correspond to those associated with the CAR and CCR algebras, respectively. Building on this foundation, we devise a construction that links CCR and CAR algebras to a unified sL algebra via a Cuntz-Toeplitz framework, thus providing an alternative method to the standard fermionic and bosonic quantization procedures. Additionally, we discuss how the locality property in systems described by the CAR, CCR algebras can be explained by the conjugate symmetry actions. Moreover, the structure of continuous analogues of these algebras, such as the $q$-Boson and $q$-fermion algebras, are captured through the Cuntz-Toeplitz framework at the level of isometry representations.

This report presents a novel minor-step operational semantics for GP 2, incorporating elements of structural congruence and reduction. Building upon a previously established denotational semantics, this new semantics should provide insight into GP 2's computation model and serve as a foundation for further research into programming GP 2 programs.

Investigating how young stars release gas is essential to understanding their early propeller activity and long-term peaceful state. Two key theories behind this release are disk breezes driven by magnetic forces and stellar wind affecting disk gases. Upcoming observations of the TW Hydrae young star system, which is easily detectable due to its proximity, will shed more light on these release processes through multi-frequency radio wave observations. These new observations, coupled with existing data on the star system, can help determine the rates at which gases are leaving the disk and the sizes of the star's outer boundary, providing crucial insights into the dynamics of young star systems.

We address the challenge of factoring and expanding Chebyshev polynomials in a different manner. Rather than utilizing the formula $u^2 - 2u \cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})+1$ to solve for $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$, we first introduce a quadratic equation with a coefficient of $\alpha$ for $-2\pi/d$, and then determine the optimal value of $\alpha$ that leads to factorizations of Chebyshev polynomials with the fewest possible equations. By employing this novel method, we derive new insights into Chebyshev polynomial factorizations, and also discover that the optimal value of $\alpha$ allows us to facilitate computations of $d$-th roots of unity and fractions thereof. As the optimal value of $\alpha$ causes the constant term of the given quadratic equation to shift by $1$, it enables us to also devise a method for computing $d$-th roots of unity and fractions thereof. Additionally, we propose an algorithm to automatically find optimal variants of $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ for factoring and expanding Chebyshev polynomials, and demonstrate that there are many more methods for factoring and expanding these polynomials than we previously thought. In particular, we show that the existence of these additional methods is evident in interesting ways from a recent paper by Forster and Sironi, and also observe that the existence of these additional

The existing research on anti-fishing and anti-resonance control methods for two-core symmetric transformers is reviewed, and existing limitations in maintaining detection accuracy during transients are acknowledged. A novel detection method with enhanced accuracy and categorization of transients is presented, along with a modular structure that facilitates adaptation to various anti-fishing and anti-resonance control schemes. The proposed method's reliability is validated through testing on a transformer model.

To achieve the high data rates required for fifth-generation (5G) services like virtual and augmented reality, unlicensed millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication holds promise. Multi-group broadcast applications, such as delivering the same information to various security clearance levels in 5G military services, pose problems for mmWave networks due to limited coverage and high noise levels. Although advanced encoding methods can improve network capacity for such broadcasts, they have limitations in mmWave environments with multiple groups. Our approach introduces a hybrid encoding strategy, combining multi-group broadcast capacity enhancement with low error rates and high spectrum efficiency in mmWave networks. A hybrid scheme consisting of sparse code multiple access and low density parity check is proposed, optimized through a constrained covariance matrix estimation problem. Our results demonstrate that this hybrid scheme surpasses the performance of existing low density parity check and multi-group broadcast coding methods.

Given an element g of finite order in a free group F, this paper's primary goal is to understand how the set of finite presentations producing g as the fundamental group's generator relates to its word metric. Additional fundermental questions include: Is the set of such presentations inherently complex? Can it be mathematically described through a simple, automatic formula? Does the size of this set fluctuate predictably based on the size of g? These questions lead to further, even more intricate questions spanning the boundaries between algebra, geometry, and number theory. Our approach involves a blend of geometric, algebraic, and number-theoretic methodologies. These results have been extended to a broader application: the solutions to all the described questions in a natural context of groups, namely, the biorderable Artin groups on four edges.

We lay out the material and structural properties of a star-shaped graph composed of three edges with varying lengths, subject to uniform density, which facilitates uniform Young's modulus throughout the structure. Next, we establish the stability criteria for an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam on this multi-branched graph and investigate how the tip displacements of its extremity vertices impact stability. Additionally, we explore the influence of tip displacements on stability when subjected to dynamic forces, examining phase trajectories in the process.

Investigations into nuclear reactions via machine learning depend heavily on the accuracy of the input data, particularly for the fast neutron capture process that plays a crucial role in $r$-process nucleosynthesis. A recent study using the TPC-1 reaction theory calculated the cross-sections of the involved isotopes with precision, and we utilize this data to train artificial neural networks for the first time, alongside a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network, to predict nuclear weights. The accuracy of the two machine learning models is then compared to existing theoretical calculations. Based on the network predictions, we map out the nuclear divide according to the calculated nuclear thickness parameter $\sigma_v$ and outline the future scope for these algorithms in nuclear physics.

Superconducting qubit performance is limited by photon flux in radiofrequency and microwave frequency ranges, primarily due to dielectric dissipation rather than other factors. Since sapphire is a widely used dielectric material in qubit implementation, its dissipation properties have been extensively examined at lower frequencies. Recent results indicate that sapphire's dissipation decreases as the frequency approaches the terahertz range. To examine this trend in the quantum frequency regime with high precision, we employed a dual-parallel measurement approach comparing the Q factors of identical qubits with and without their cryogenic tanks removed. Q-factor measurements of 700 and 300 were recorded at 7 GHz using two methods, demonstrating the existence of a Q factor difference of 400 parts per billion. This measurement accuracy surpasses all previous tests of sapphire's dissipation, with a relative error of less than 5%.

The potential pull experienced by light traveling through a medium is described mathematically by a simple formula derived from Maxwell's equations, with an empirical adjustment if necessary to account for non-uniformity. However, when pull is significantly stronger than push, this formula yields an inaccurate approximation for certain cases. In this study, we examine these instances within a linearized context, specifically in regimes without propagation, where a more detailed analysis based on Maxwell's equations reveals a more complex relationship involving medium geometry and polarization. We demonstrate that this new understanding is applicable to and provides new insights within two contrasting scenarios, namely the critical layer with infinitesimally thin slabs and electromagnetic induction in cavity electromagnetics with highly resonant cavities.

Two-stage optimization planning has been used to manage uncertainty in various problems. Continuity and convexity constraints have been a focus for recent theoretical developments, but the lack of dual information for binary variables is a significant limitation. This paper introduces a Lagrangian dual-based method to handle problems with binary variables in the second stage, yielding a tractable solution under certain conditions. It's noted that implementing this method globally is computationally challenging due to non-convexity, so an efficient method for finding a reliable, initial solution is instead provided, along with a case study of demand response in energy management.

The comprehensive nature of datasets in the field of computer vision, which includes datasets such as ImageNet and COCO, has significantly contributed to the advancement of related research fields. To bridge the gap between vision and socioeconomic research, a new dataset called H4M is introduced, which is characterized by its diversity in four aspects: diversity stemming from various demographic groups, diversity in data sources, diversity in formats of data, and diversity in origins. H4M, specifically designed for socioeconomic research in Beijing, consists of four categories of images and includes a total of 12,000 high-quality images as well as 5,000 poor-quality images. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this new dataset by applying different pre-training methods to the four categories, which reveals variations in performance patterns. Our research also uses the developed dataset to propose novel research directions, which include researching the ability of models to adapt to different formats and origins, as well as exploring the origin of the bias that exists within deep neural networks.

The quantity of data in various sciences and engineering has experienced exponential growth. This surge has led to a new era where data analysis yields hypotheses which need to be constantly verified. Consequently, a substantial rise in the number of tests has been observed, resulting in an alarming issue of a large dataset requiring continuous investigation. Moreover, the incredibly large dimensions of today's data pose significant challenges to the application of traditional and state-of-the-art data analysis methods. To address this problem, a visualisation-based approach is presented which integrates data reduction techniques to efficiently handle large datasets and extract valuable insights from them. The proposed method, known as visual template-driven investigation of data, employs a semi-automatic approach to perform reliable multiple tests on a dataset. The effectiveness and efficiency of this method have been demonstrated through its successful application in various scientific and engineering studies, including meteorology, astronomy, and materials science.

Many graph neural networks (GNNs) have been developed to achieve state-of-the-art performance on node and graph classification tasks. It's crucial to understand how these GNNs transfer knowledge between interconnected nodes to facilitate task adaptation and requirements. Through in-depth analysis, we have explored the transfer patterns of various GNN architectures, including traditional and graph augmentation-based methods, on five significant node classification datasets. Our research reveals that older GNN architectures with basic structures exhibit significant inter-node connectivity, whereas newer, more sophisticated methods demonstrate weaker associations between interconnected nodes. Moreover, graph augmentation techniques do not inherently guarantee reduced node connectivity. The underlying architectural characteristics of these methods, particularly their tendency to concentrate similar nodes together, are found to be the primary cause of improved transfer patterns.

As the internet continues to expand globally, the sheer volume of information available has reached catastrophic proportions, leading to a common issue among users: the overwhelming amount of data makes it difficult to pinpoint relevant information. Consequently, various suggestion services have emerged to provide personalized recommendations and streamline users' lives. This article focuses on a specific type of suggestion system known as the dual feature distribution model, which enables user items mapping and incorporates both user and item factors to generate recommendations. This innovative method utilizes a unique model to address the homogeneity problem and a sampling strategy to tackle the heterogeneity issue. Additionally, two improved DFDM models are proposed to further enhance performance, with empirical validation demonstrating their superiority over conventional approaches.

The problem of determining whether there's a single binary string that results from a series of disjoint set operations was previously shown to have an optimal solution of O(n) space over an n-bit string. This result is achieved by combining two straightforward algorithms - Linial's algorithm, first described in 1990, and a simple negation-based approach. This solution has been known for 30 years, yet it is still relatively underutilized. Our goal here is to document this proof because it presents a straightforward and easy-to-understand method for solving the disjointness problem, even though more advanced and complex solutions exist. Furthermore, this technique has additional value in data stream processing where it can be utilized to develop algorithms for resolving decision-making issues.

We calculate the spin stiffness based on a non-linear momentum representation, which was developed by Hymenite and Luscombe. We show that the spin stiffness derived from their work has a unique momentum dependence and relies on higher-order Taylor series terms beyond those of $k^2$. This contrasts with our previously established analytic form, which captures the $k^2$ dependence accurately but fails to account for these additional terms. Given that the magnetization and spin stiffness are closely intertwined, we suspect that the magnetization's small-$k$ expansion, which relies on a quadratic term, may also be incorrect. This discrepancy could explain why existing numerical calculations of the magnetization's expansion have not aligned with our predicted cubic term. If this interpretation holds, it may indicate a critical shift in the renormalization group flow of three-dimensional Heisenberg magnets towards a trivial fixed point, which would result in a lack of critical exponents within the mean-field approximation framework.

The discovery of multiple qubit entanglement is typically indicative of a quantum system's presence. However, conventional multiple qubit entanglement detection methods often require a long, coherent storage time, making them unsuitable for many atomic systems. This issue is resolved using a new method that relies on multi-diffraction interference instead. This method can detect the presence of a single atom and determine its position by analyzing the diffraction pattern of a stored atom, exceeding the typical resolution limit. Additionally, we propose using multi-pulse Rabi oscillations to increase the atom-photon interaction, thereby enabling the projective measurement of a single atom, even when it's in an unknown state, without compromising the atom's storage coherence. This technique, dubbed multi-diffraction design, is more efficient than single-atom spectroscopy and detection using entangled atoms, and does not require entanglement. Hence, it provides an alternative approach to developing atomic storage, manipulation, and measurement platforms.

In systems exhibiting symmetry breaking, where time-reversal symmetry is present but not inherent, a specific type of conductivity called the Hall conductivity is seen, especially in two-dimensional systems. This study focuses on a specific type of system where this symmetry is present but not inherent, and it uses a complex system that is chaotic and interacting to determine the Hall conductivity. This study finds that even in a highly complex system where determinants are calculated, there is a clear, predictable formula for linear conductivity. However, this study also shows that when there is a relationship between frequency and momentum, there are corrections to the Hall conductivity. This correction is linked to a complex phenomenon that is known to be associated with chaos and interactions. This correction is part of a broader structure of conductivity that includes both linear and nonlinear components. This study further supports these findings by showing that when there are no exceptions, these formulas for conductivity are clear and predictable. Finally, this study also shows that even when the model for this system is changed, the formulas for conductivity are still valid and remain universal.

To expedite the process of incorporating new knowledge into AI models, an immediate transcription phase is required. Our proposed strategy is to leverage massive pre-trained models of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate high-quality transcriptions and enhance them via GAN-guided correction, followed by fine-tuning. We have successfully applied this method to a dual-patient conversation scenario during the COVID-19 pandemic, obtaining impressive results within a minimal timeframe. Our approach effectively reduces the latency between new knowledge integration and model updating, addressing the tidality issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that despite some initial performance degradation, our model can seamlessly pivot to generate more accurate transcriptions after a brief period.

We are studying the platform groups, a concept introduced by Keith Bradshaw, 
associated with iterations of bicritical rational functions. Our findings reveal 
that for bicritical postsurgery groups of type $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, the platform 
group of an appropriately defined iterated map corresponds to the original 
group. Additionally, for a given bicritical map $f$, the corresponding 
platform groups of its iterated functions can be generated by a real number, 
satisfying a specific inequality.

The properties of two-dimensional semiconducting Mo and W dichalcogenides are thoroughly examined through computational models, leveraging DFT and GW methods to explore electronic characteristics and chemical reactions. Our analysis suggests that changing the dichalcogenide composition alters their electrostatic properties on a macroscopic scale, leading to contrasting behaviors within these semiconducting materials. For example, as the composition changes, the semiconducting gap/stable electron work function ratio fluctuates, while the ionization gap/total electron work function ratio remains relatively constant. Additionally, our findings indicate that the semiconducting gap/total electron work function is generally non-negligible in comparison to the semiconcting gap/gap energy, which is largely influenced by the dichalcogenide composition's 2D characteristics. Observations on the energy per particle and macroscopic properties further support this, underscoring the importance of considering thickness effects in two-dimensional materials' properties.

A novel framework, universal supervised learning, is presented as a series of steps to train a neural network, modeled after existing algorithms, to accurately replicate learning processes for different neural networks and various data sets through a dynamic selection process of training methods and techniques. This concept is developed by applying a series of dynamic filters, known as delta lenses, to a neural network's computational process, thereby evolving the standard backpropagation algorithm in a universal direction. This research showcases the effectiveness of universal learning through a range of experiments in which a universal backpropagation algorithm is trained on data from multiple source platforms and is able to efficiently learn and apply its skills on various target platforms, outperforming traditional backpropagation in some cases.

A variation of the constant phase approximation is being examined where phase profiles belong to the Lp norm for a specific range of p values between 1 and infinity, under a Lipschitz constraint. By doing so, we can preserve a key property of the original constant phase approximation, which is the ability to map an interval to a circle up to homeomorphism. Our work will also delve into the following topics: the relationship between our approximation and a class of distributions introduced by T. Bagchi et al., an extension of our approximation to higher dimensions, an exploration of its relation to Fourier series, and a demonstration of its application in establishing uniform bounds on periodic solutions within a specific class of Schrodinger equations.

Using the direct numerical simulation approach, we investigate the convergence of steady-state solutions for different rarefied gas flow scenarios across various time cycles and different model levels of simplification. Specifically, we focus on a gas flow through a 2D channel with perpendicular plates, a scenario where the flow may experience bounces and (thermal) slip conditions. Our study assesses the role of model assumptions versus initial conditions on the calculation of steady-state flow profiles, as well as the relationship between flow speed and boundary layer thickness. It appears that initiating the simulation from a uniform fluid in the channel minimizes the time to reach a steady-state solution, though this can depend on the specific model level of simplification. Furthermore, we examine the potential of the iterative solution algorithm to reach steady-state solutions within a shorter simulation time when an appropriate initial profile is used, alongside evaluating the suitability of particular models for this type of flow scenario.

The Horizon-10T experiment reported a phenomenon known as "Multiple Unidirectional Rings" (MUR) which poses difficulties in its explanation. While the phenomenon could be linked to the interaction of neutrinos and electrons with the Earth's surface, another plausible cause might be related to the emission of light axion particles in the vicinity of the Earth. Since these hypothetical particles are extremely weakly interacting, their presence is further substantiated by observations from Axion Quark Particle (AQP) that utilizes the full solid angle in observation. Recent analyses by AQP have reported occurrences of "Large Events" (LE) and "Small Events" (SE) that are distinguished based on the number of observed photomultiplier tubes (PMT) involved. Both the Horizon-10T MUR and AQP's SE have similarities with the predicted characteristics of SE events. Furthermore, SE events have certain features that are thought to correspond with the gravitational wave from the merger of neutron stars. Analyses of both Horizon-10T MUR and AQP's SE suggest that they belong to a class known as "Low-Mass Dark Matter" (LMDM) in which numerous events are detected consecutively from different Unidirectional Rings (UR). However, both the "Single High-Mass" (SHM) and "Multi-Mass" (MM) classes have not been ruled out as alternatives to LMDM. Statistical distribution of Horizon-10T MUR and AQP's

The CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has collected data for almost six years, which has been utilized to study the two-photon decay pattern of a hypothetical Higgs-like particle discovered in 2012. By combining a reduced dataset of 36.5 fb^-1, which was collected in 2011 with higher energy proton-proton collisions, the research further examines the Higgs-like particle's characteristics in the 125 GeV range. The findings from this study represent a nearly 4.2 standard deviation increase, which was initially observed in a smaller dataset. Furthermore, by comparing the Higgs-like particle's production efficiency with that of predicted models, the research finds no significant discrepancies. Specifically, the Higgs-like particle's properties in terms of spin, CP properties, and compatibility with the Standard Model were investigated, with the goal of determining if its behavior aligns with the Standard Model's expectations or if it exhibits deviations that could be observed this year. By combining the measured cross-sections of top-quark pairs with bottom-quark pairs and top-quark and bottom-quark combinations, the research found that these particles' relative occurrence relative to the predicted Standard Model values showed no significant deviations, with a 1.4 standard deviation increase. The research also explored the correlation between Higgs-like particle data and its predicted low-momentum transverse momentum, with the goal of understanding the underlying physics in the process. The research found that this correlation exhibited no significant deviations

For a Siegel modular form $\phi$ of weight $2k$, let $\psi$ be the Fourier parameter at a cusp associated with a parabolic subgroup of $Sp_{2n}(Z_p)$ and denote its $p$-adic valuation by $\nu_p(\psi)$ and the wild archimedian contribution by $\lambda_{\infty}(\psi)$. Assuming $\phi$ has a normalised Schwartz Whittaker function, we show that its Fourier parameter satisfies the relation $\lambda_{\infty(\psi)} = -2^{n-k} \nu_p(\psi)$. As a result, the Fourier parameter $\psi$ must have a $p$-adic valuation that is at least $n-k$ in magnitude. Additionally, the study includes a detailed examination of the contribution $\lambda_{\infty(\psi)}$ to the Fourier parameter $\psi$ and its relation to the generic representation of $\phi$.

Two types of fibration sequences, the product fibrations and stiff fibrations, have been linked to a precise relationship by Hitotsumatsu, Nishida, and Shimakawa. Our research establishes a further connection, stating that a sequence of stiff fibrations leads to a sequence of product fibrations, which in turn provides a sequence of real polynomials, enabling us to apply the theory of infinite words and Ramsey theory to count them. This counting can be used to determine the homotopy types of certain spaces associated with the fibrations and to find bounds for the difference between the volumes of these spaces and a product volume constructed from their base and fibers.

To develop a physical understanding of the 2D Pauli structure, a formalism is introduced that generalizes the scalar product of two vectors to the space of quadratic forms. This is achieved by a single parameter, K, which acts as a scale factor. Beyond its own relevance, this approach has broader implications for theoretical research, particularly in structures theory.

Neural networks are extensively employed in numerous applications such as function approximation and classification, however their potential to tackle time-varying issues remains understudied. Conventional approaches can no longer meet the demand for accurate modeling as processes become increasingly complex and dynamic. To effectively forecast time-dependent changes in systems, particularly in matrix-related problems, an intriguing forecast method has emerged but has been largely overlooked in the research community. Despite its significant contributions, the underlying theory of this approach is shrouded in mystery. Therefore, a comprehensive examination of its fundamental principles is long overdue. Through the creation of a novel forecasting method based on the ZNN technique, the book delves into the world of matrix challenges that require forecasting to be within a acceptable threshold, addressing the question, what must a matrix look like to ensure its eigenvalues satisfy a given constraint? Additionally, the book discovers new representations for Polya frequency sequence-based functions, which have been overlooked in the literature, and develops the first-ever forecasting method utilizing neural networks to solve this problem.

The edge-detecting 'on-off' center-surround vision of mammals has guided the growth of deep neural networks, suggesting the presence of similar vision mechanisms in computers could enhance their performance. Drawing inspiration from biologically plausile mechanisms, we have developed a novel 'on-off' center-surround network for image classification tasks. Our research shows that incorporating this network as an input feature for a classification model accurately pinpointed sensitive image areas, thereby improving the model's overall accuracy and image classification robustness to noise. The model outperforms current state-of-the-art models in image classification.

X-ray optics with higher angular resolution provide sharper, larger-scale images of celestial sources and intricate structures, though this usually comes at the expense of collecting area. To balance both, a new approach called "asymmetric techniques" has been devised for various types of X-ray optics, including mirrors, grids, and arrays. These techniques can significantly enhance an X-ray telescope's capabilities without compromising its key features. This study focuses on the specifics of these techniques and their potential outcomes for large-scale X-ray telescopes and tables, detailing relevant experiments and evaluations. We also examine the various approaches to implementing these techniques in existing and upcoming experiments, such as the large-scale X-ray Overhead Spectrometric Experiment (XOSE), the large-scale X-ray Astrophysical Observatory (XAO), and other potential space-based missions.

To examine the continuum model of twisted bilayer graphene, we analyze the phase generated by the velocity of electrons under a $2\pi$ flux change. We locate the points where this phase becomes irrational, causing the continuum model to break down, and observe that they coincide with the boundaries of flat-band regions seen in the exact wavefunction. We show that regions with an irrational phase exhibit chiral properties and electrodynamics similar to those found in fractal patterns formed by integer quantum Hall states. We find that the continuum model fails to accurately predict the locations of all flat bands and instead selects specific flat bands based on the phase's irrationality. The relationship between these phases and the model's predictability is conserved even when the flux reaches values beyond $2\pi$.

Our research focuses on hidden information within specific music genres, uncovering an intriguing phenomenon where certain types of music naturally conceal melodies. We aim to understand the structure of these hidden melodies and the underlying patterns by analyzing music from two distinct databases. Our investigation reveals that hidden melodies exhibit a distinctive repeating pattern in their sequences. Building upon this discovery, we develop an LSTM-based model to predict these hidden melodies. Our design of this neural network draws inspiration from an LSTM that generates music, incorporating a specific mechanism to mimic the repeating structure. Our analysis verifies the significance of this design element and demonstrates that an enhanced LSTM can accurately recreate the hidden melodies, both locally and in completed songs. This finding could lead to the development of an advanced technique to conceal information within music.

The goal of unit commitment (UC) is to efficiently operate a power grid by determining which generating units should be online at any given moment. One of the challenges with UC is the complex compliance framework that varies by region and operator, causing delays and hindrances in solving the complex optimization problem. Our proposed approach can quickly and accurately assess compliance with operational constraints by training a cost model using historical data, significantly improving the efficiency of UC solutions. This cost model can be used to identify non-feasible solutions, and with a slight enhancement, can even detect infeasibility with greater accuracy, all without requiring underlying optimization software. Our results indicate that our cost model can effectively identify infeasibility with a high level of precision, and that the subsequent calculation of compliance violations can be completed within a reasonable timeframe. Moreover, our model exhibits adaptable performance, allowing it for its use to be both restricted and unrestricted. When the model's cost estimates are compared to actual UC solutions, we find that its predictions demonstrate impressive correlation with actual UC solutions, particularly for various regional settings and different spans of historical data. Consequently, our model holds significant promise for facilitating efficient and accurate UC solutions.

Our investigation using ab initio constant stress simulations was conducted on 
alpha-Li2IrO3 under stress conditions that cause volume reduction. We observed 
that initial applied compressive stress below 0.5 GPa generates dimerization 
stress closely resembling that found at the N\'eel temperature. It's noteworthy 
that this dimerization consistently arises under decreasing volume, regardless 
of stress orientation, and correlates with increased effective exchange energies 
related to crystal orientation. Interestingly, a moderate level of 0.5 GPa 
compressive stress stabilizes the antiferromagnetic order past the N\'eel point, 
and our study demonstrates that this stabilization results from increased Heisenberg 
exchange within iridium atoms, thereby supporting the proposed Kitaev nature 
of alpha-Li2IrO3. Furthermore, our results illustrate a mechanism where failure 
of magnetism in these compounds is often linked to a physical process where 
stress-induced dimerization raises the exchange energies, thereby shifting the 
balance towards antiferromagnetic order, a phenomenon that can occur without 
satisfying the condition for a topological gap. Lastly, our study shows that 
mechanical properties significantly influence the electronic properties of these 
materials, and this influence likely extends to a broad range of related 
materials.

The synthetic control method is widely used for assessing the effect of a treatment introduced for a single unit by comparing the treated entity to a weighted average of untreated units that resemble the treated entity in terms of past outcomes and other relevant characteristics. This note develops a theoretical framework for the synthetic control method by viewing it as a form of nearest neighbor causal inference in a structured set of potential outcomes. By making regularity assumptions regarding the data distribution, the estimators for average and local treatment effects are shown to converge at varying rates of convergence determined by a measure of distance between treated and untreated observations. These findings are applied to establish the convergence rates for the specific synthetic control estimators based on nearest neighbor and k-nearest neighbor methods. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method can handle non-normal data and outliers more effectively than traditional methods. Local linear regression results obtained from applying the method to U.S. state-level data to examine the impact of joining the European Union on U.S. state economic performance are also presented.

Gromov-Wasserstein divergence has been widely used in graph-based data analysis for assessing similarity between nodes within different graphs with varying dimensions. This study enhances the GW divergence by integrating multiple graphs and incorporates a secure communication system, specifically noise-reducing GW divergence that guarantees the protection of sensitive data, while demonstrating the uniqueness of the revised method. Furthermore, simulations have been conducted to compare the new method with existing graph-based divergence methods that ensure data confidentiality.

Recent high-energy laser and plasma interactions have driven significant advances in plasma physics and physics of high-energy processes, yielding numerous groundbreaking findings. A new theoretical study focuses on the interaction between an extremely powerful, arbitrarily polarized laser beam and a faint plasma, taking into consideration the laser's instantaneous steepening effect due to its interaction with the plasma. This investigation examines in detail the complex spatial and temporal patterns of electron injection and high-energy bending within the plasma when triggered by a laser beam of any polarization orientation and energy intensity, delivered in a brief, intense pulse. By using advanced simulations involving Maxwell-Vlasov equations, this study provides new insights into how the laser's polarization impacts these processes and how the resulting electron energy distributions are affected by both the laser's polarization and energy intensity in an independent manner. These energy-driven electron distributions consist of a standard bump and various distinct bumps formed through a series of complex nonlinear interactions between the laser and plasma, yielding a correlated pattern of electron high-energy processes over time. These findings may have important implications for understanding and predicting a wide range of phenomena in laser-plasma interactions, including electron high-energy processes, their bifurcation, and memory effects in nonlinear regime.

To investigate possible connections between the elements platinum and dark matter, researchers examine various processes in the presence of nuclei characterized by large neutron-proton disparities. Specifically, they consider the elements platinum-100 and platinum-102, providing updated bounds on their spontaneous double beta decay in the presence of dark matter and proposing innovative links between the elements platinum and dark matter through interactions facilitated by scalar, vector, and tensor mediators. In addition, new signatures of dark matter are suggested for the study of double beta decay at future experiments.

The renormalization of the flavor-singlet axial-vector current charge, along with its associated anomaly in QCD, has been calculated using a method called dimensional regularization in a special type of equation called a bare bubble diagram. This analysis includes a comprehensive examination of various special cases such as massless scattering, various types of massive particle scattering, and the behavior of these charges at high energy levels. A key component of this work involves deriving the values of several important constants, such as the QCD charge, and the coefficients of a high-energy expansion called the renormalization group in theories where all particles have equal weight, or "equivalent" theories. This work further builds on previous similar calculations by removing a type of error that occurs in calculations, and providing an alternative solution to a particular problem with the standard QCD equation that involves an infinite series of complex numbers called an asymptotic series.

We introduce a novel approach, Dubeltos, to the challenging task of colorizing black and white video by leveraging the collaborative advantages of processing multiple frames from different cameras. As each camera captures a unique perspective, we adopt a multi-camera framework where the color information is shared among them. This methodology not only improves the output of individual frames but also maintains consistency across the video sequence, facilitating seamless cross-camera colorization. To achieve this, we propose an innovative architecture that allows the colorization of simultaneous frames from multiple cameras, where the color predictions are generated jointly and refined through mutual influence. This method effectively utilizes paired multi-camera datasets to enhance colorization capabilities. We evaluate our approach on datasets like the "Dudek Pedestrian" video and the iconic black and white footage of Apollo 11 from NASA, demonstrating the efficacy of our multi-camera collaboration method in producing detailed and realistic colorized video. This research is presented at the International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) 2021.

The Ermakov System in two dimensions has been extended to n dimensions, with a corresponding Hamiltonian and symmetries identified. A conservation law was also discovered which involves the Poisson bracket. A particular note is made of the fact that one of the conserved quantities in 2D is missing in n dimensions, however, it's observed that one is restored when the system reduces to one dimension.

The way that ride-hailing and ride-sharing services operate in the majority of cities relies on transport feed, a type of data that estimates pickup and drop-off locations for a large number of users. Existing algorithms used for predicting ride-demand typically require precise spatial data, but face difficulties when dealing with incomplete ride-feed data, often provided in cities. To address this challenge, we propose a new type of neural network model that can process ride-feed data at a higher level and work effectively even with incomplete data. By using ride-feed information that specifies the routes that riders use, as well as their pickup and drop-off locations, we can train this model to estimate the distribution of future ride requests across different areas. To achieve this, we transform the available ride-feed data into a more consistent format using a pre-processing technique, often called the Unavailable Transport Feed Specification. By repeatedly applying this technique, we can improve the accuracy of our neural network model estimates. At a cost that is comparable to existing methods, our proposed model can accurately predict ride-demand even when it is applied to cities where the ride-feed data is incomplete. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we tested it using data from the cities of New York and San Francisco, and found that it accurately predicted ride-demand and significantly outperformed existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both scenarios.

In the realm of few-shot classification, standard prototypes that account for individual training examples tend to fall short when dealing with a plethora of categories. To counteract this limitation, we propose learning category-specific prototypes by aggregating features from interested training samples within each class. Nevertheless, this task is hindered by two hurdles. Firstly, prototypes are susceptible to outliers which can disrupt feature calculations. Secondly, categories exhibiting significant diversity may result in poorly representative features due to the potential dominance of specific regional features over others, as seen for example in the case of a bird category where the features of the face, wings, and beak are often overlapping.

To effectively learn such prototypes while managing the influence of outliers and catering to features that represent central tendencies in categorical data, we have developed an innovative prototype learning framework. Notably, by adopting a variational distance metric that measures the similarity between a prototype and a distribution representing a category's essential characteristics, we have successfully implicitly excluded outliers and promoted robust feature learning. Furthermore, we have effectively learned class-level features, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-size-fits-all prototypes, while exploring ways to reduce the impact of noisy regional features by modeling the variance of features within each class. Experimental results from multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of this proposed framework over existing methods.

We're analyzing systems that have an underlying non-reversible group of symmetries, which can be locally expounded via a real, non-Abelian Lie group $G$, with its associated Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. Assuming that a certain condition, known as the non-Local Burgers equation condition, is met, it's shown that a local operator $O$ adheres to the property $\Delta O = \mathfrak{g}$. This holds true both locally and temporally, with the result generalized for functions that have a certain profile. This proof relies on non-Abelian and non-reversible symmetry, with the latter stipulating that the group of symmetries doesn't need to conform to any simple constraint, as is typical of certain systems. It's further shown that a local equivalent of Noether's theorem can be formulated, with the result encompassing both non-Abelian and non-reversible symmetry. A number of systems that fall under this category have been identified, with the non-Local Burgers equation being a prime example. Other systems including non-reversible superconductivity, classical Klein-Gordon models, and certain types of non-Abelian solitons also fit within this framework, with certain specific examples providing a clearer illustration of the result.

A semi-transitive graph, defined as a non-directed graph where any triplet of connected nodes results in a transitive relationship, has been studied and applied in various fields, including biology, yet a related fully transitive graph structure challenge has remained unresolved since first proposed in 1982. A new effort seeks to resolve this by demonstrating a specific limit on the construction of fully transitive split graphs, showing that a maximum of n^(1.3496) can be formed, though a more optimized variant fails to identify a polynomial bound.

In particle physics, identifying how tau particles decay is a critical task that has been challenging to solve for decades. Researchers have recently employed deep neural networks (DNN) to tackle this problem, which involves analyzing complex data from tau lepton decays in particle collisions. A proposed method uses a DNN to recognize tau particle formations, which is evaluated based on simulated data from particle collisions. By incorporating global symmetry, this technique can effectively recognize combined particle formations in three-dimensional situations. Utilizing simulated data from particle collisions, it has been demonstrated that the DNN method is capable of accurately recognizing tau particle formations when the underlying components are fully known, even when the components are viewed in various angles. Additionally, the proposed DNN approach is able, although not perfect, recognized tau particle formations when the underlying components are fully unknown, with a reported accuracy rate of 70%. By integrating this method into particle collision experiments, it is anticipated that it can significantly contribute to particle physics research by accurately analyzing tau particle formations. As a result of this innovation, it is predicted that the proposed DNN approach will greatly enhance our comprehension of particle physics, particularly in the investigation of tau particle formations.

Upcoming studies with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are set to significantly boost the number of accessible photometric data, enabling more precise classifications of supernovae and other significant astrophysical events. One key aspect of these classifications involves near-infrared color information, which is often hindered by technical limitations. Twin challenges arise in high-redshift supernovae and Transient Angle Monitor (TMON) transients, primarily volume effects and noise in near-infrared data, although a promising approach uses dual neural network architectures to mitigate near-infrared shortages. This research extends this concept by employing a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) model to monitor transients for the most image-intensive events, aiming to improve the likelihood of accurate high-redshift supernova and TMON classifications through more robust photometric predictions. Additionally, we explore the BNN model's potential to mitigate near-infrared color shortages by assessing the optimal number of required bands based on a comprehensive photometric database. Our study compares the performance of BNN and traditional machine learning models, and the differences and similarities will be discussed along with an examination of the BNN model's potential applications in Rubin era data, specifically a proposed system for the most image-intensive TMON transients that leverages near and far paste data for improved supernova and transients categorization.

Our study presents a technique for detecting modulation and interaction between modes 
in photonic crystal fibers with a solid core and cladding using the Brillouin effect.
This technique can accurately measure the difference in modulation frequencies 
between different modes within the fiber, known as AFg. The corresponding gain band 
varies depending on the involved modes and frequency coupling. Theoretical models 
indicate that the frequency difference between distinct modes is directly related 
to the fiber's geometric characteristics. Furthermore, the technique enables the 
identification of mechanical mode symmetries by analyzing how mode frequencies 
relate to one another. The observed effects demonstrate strong modal coupling 
during mechanical stimulation. The unique characteristics of photonic crystal fibers 
with solid cores allow for the observation of mechanical meta-material properties 
affecting light propagation.

The Coxeter group foundation theorem, primarily studied in solvable groups, states that any minimal generating set of a solvable Coxeter group naturally divides into two sets: one consisting of arbitrary elements and another consisting entirely of 2-elements. We will expand on this concept to cover all B-type Coxeter groups. In doing so, we will introduce a concept called 'basic generating sets', establish a quick method to verify if a Coxeter graph is automatically associated with such generating sets, and further demonstrate how to construct a basic generating set of a Coxeter group given a basic generating set of its quotient group in the case where the quotient group is solvable.

The 2021 Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem at ICML is a two-stage optimization problem.
First, it selects items from a given set to cover as much of the data as possible within a budget, at an initial stage called the selection stage.
Then, at the packing stage, the optimally selected items are packed to the best extent possible, at a budget not exceeding the selection stage.
Our solution for the problem is a novel combination of steps called effective-and-efficient local search.
It employs a simple iterative algorithm to improve the selection and packing of items from the given set.
Using the model and dataset provided with the submitted source code, our solution achieves the best known performance on the given dataset problem at both stages, at a computational cost that greatly exceeds the time it takes to process each data point individually.
As a result, our solution at the packing stage includes all the packed items when using an optimally selected subset of items from the given dataset.

It is worth noting that the best known performance was achieved after manually tuning the parameters of our solution to accurately solve the problem at both stages, at a computational cost that greatly exceeded the time it takes to process each data point individually. 
However, the main idea behind our solution is to apply a novel technique of enhancing intermediate results from the first stage to accurately solve the problem at both stages.
