This method involves selecting a subset of relevant variables by comparing treatments to a control condition. While our results show that the proposed statistical method can accurately predict causal effects for certain scenarios, they also indicate that there are substantial limitations to finding the boundaries for nonparametric causal inference, especially in cases with complex relationships between variables. Even using the most effective approaches, such as those utilizing Bayesian or frequentist statistical methods for selecting variables, there are strict limitations to finding the boundaries, especially in cases with many variables. Our results apply especially to scenarios where researchers aim to understand the effects of specific variables, known as causal pins, on outcomes in cases with many variables. These restrictions may be especially relevant in numerous fields of study, such as biology and medicine, where researchers aim to understand the effects of specific variables, such as genes or drugs.

Effective protective measures for systems subject to stealthy attacks are presented, handled as separate defense strategies that must be decided upon in advance, one of which involves using sensors to monitor the system and detect anomalies through real-time calculations on real-time data. We develop an approach for optimally designing these strategies to minimize the system's operational expenses while keeping attacks that are not detected by the sensor within a predetermined area. This method involves solving a dual optimization issue for each attack type, yielding a set of optimal effective measures that can be used across all attack types, unlike traditional methods that require separate protection schemes for each. When implementing the proposed method, it is demonstrated that it can efficiently detect rare anomalies that occur within the system and be controlled remotely without additional infrastructure. This method is further supported by case studies that demonstrate its performance in real-world settings.

A language cannot be fully grasped until its grammatical structure is thoroughly understood.
We focus on summarization using GAE to generate concise summaries of lengthy narrative texts written in Indian languages, ignoring their complex syntax. A conventional approach to automatic text summarization generates summaries using an encoder and a transformer, but our innovative method utilizes a graph-aided encoder to enhance the quality of summaries. We present GAE-ISumm, a novel, unsupervised system for improved text summarization, by leveraging a graph-aided encoder to simulate human writing styles and create well-structured summaries. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed system outperforms existing methods.

We identify Noetherian rings with the property that every left ideal has a left
component, and we prove this property characterizes such rings. Additionally, we
characterize Noetherian local rings where every left ideal has a left basis by
showing they all emerge from the quotient ring of a polynomial ring over a Noetherian
local ring with max Noetherian order, utilizing Arason's division algorithm.

The acceleration of a star is proof of a gravitational impact, typically supplied by a companion star or black hole. Stars like this, which have moved significantly in the past few decades, were found by analyzing the positions of 1,045 nearby stars from Gaia DR3 data. From this group, we pinpointed 40 stars with extreme velocity changes and isolated the causes for 23 of them, all of which involved a companion weighing at least as much as the sun. Moreover, we developed a statistical model to gauge the likelihood of an unseen companion, reaching a confidence level of 68% for 17 new instances in addition to the 26 previously documented cases in the General Catalogue of Accelerated Galactic Objects. With the aid of isochrones and a method for calculating the ages of stars, we determined the ages of 49 identified companions, with the youngest being a star accompanied by a 10-solar-mass black hole at the age of 30 million years. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the theoretical models of star-formation, with the suggestion that the presence of binary or multiple-star systems from birth may be common among our stars.

Recent advances in deep generative modeling have revealed the complexity of data distribution is enormous, causing most posterior distributions to converge towards non-interactive areas. The Bayesian autoencoder (BAE), a model that incorporates variational Bayesian learning, tends to suffer from over-specialization and over-regulation, resulting in limited interaction between its encoders and decoders. To resolve this issue, we developed a constrained BAE, incorporating the minimum square approximation objective and a regularization term, both constrained by a proximal penalty. By combining these three components, our method ensures accurate approximation of the true data distribution, standardization of latent codes, and increased interaction between the model's components. Our experimental results demonstrate improved performance over BAE, VAE, and RNVAE on image and text classification tasks.

This study introduces an innovative system for tracking IoT-based home appliances by integrating global positioning system (GPS) techniques with a private blockchain. The proposed technique addresses two primary issues for IoT security, namely location security and data integrity. Although public blockchain technology offers the benefit of immutability, its high transaction costs and slow transaction speeds often limit private blockchain adoption in security-sensitive systems. To enhance location security, we utilize a private blockchain and a GPS-based tracking method to monitor and record the location of IoT devices at regular intervals. The transaction fee is eliminated by the shared private blockchain, thereby ensuring swift and efficient tracking. The proposed method demonstrates a significant improvement in operational efficiency compared to the real-time GPS method. Furthermore, a private blockchain-based inventory management system is developed to guarantee data integrity by monitoring and managing IoT devices within a residential area. The proposed algorithms and systems are validated through simulation testing, showcasing their effectiveness under various scenarios.

A widely used compression algorithm, called gray-code encoding, connects sensors to analog-to-digital converters within analog systems to efficiently save bandwidth. This method works by converting analog input values into optimized digital output values, applying a subtle transformation. However, traditional encoding often causes problems with accuracy and latency. To resolve these issues, we developed a deeper approach to encoding by combining a deep learning model with a successful quantization technique. Our approach involves the deep learning model producing predicted logarithmic code values, L, that are then combined with the output of a quantization model to create precise Z-integers, representing the real-valued inputs, X. This method's outcome surpasses the performance of two models that traditionally tackle encoding, and demonstrates the potential to replace them. Our code can be found on the GitHub repository.

This study presents parameterized algorithms for solving the upward planarity issue, which encompasses two variants, namely consecutive overlapping convex roundtop structure and single-crossing convex roundtop structure. The upward planarity problem is defined such that, given a directed graph without cycles (a dag), a convex-roundtop structure can be obtained by placing nodes in a manner that is consistent with the direction of the edges and forms a series of convex sections. The work develops new parameterized strategies for the problem in its two forms. Specifically, it proves that the single-crossing variant is solvable in a time complex of O($n^{f(\alpha)+1}$) and demonstrates that the consecutive-overlapping variant is solvable in a time complex of $2^O((\alpha+n)/\epsilon^{\alpha}) \cdot n^{f(\alpha)+1}$, where $f(\alpha)$ describes how the number of sections grows with the number of nodes, a value less than $\alpha$; $\epsilon$ is a value greater than zero indicating the separation bound; and the time complexity is determined by an L-reduction to the multicolour graph-bicompactness problem, a problem solved by Bodlaender. The study further improves upon previous single-crossing convex roundtop structure solvers by reducing the time complexity, simplifying the approach by eliminating the need for a flow augmentation and using an L-reduction instead. For the consecutive-overlapping variant, it builds upon previous single-crossing

Crowdsourced measurements with high noise levels pose significant difficulties due to the inclusion of both relevant and irrelevant data points. Current methods provide limited success in addressing this problem, primarily reducing the impact of noise but failing to fully capture genuine label data. In particular, the widely used Maximum Vote algorithm still relies on extraneous annotations. We now present an innovative approach, leveraging the diverse opinions of crowdsource workers as probabilistic inputs rather than discarding them. This method involves combining individual probabilities with a soft maximum, followed by the application of an ensemble model for refined classification. Notably, our scheme also enables the calculation of a label's reliability and provides an accurate estimate of the amount of trustworthy data available. This study showcases the efficacy of our method through experimental validation using images of Chest X-Rays, a field with strict regulatory requirements for diagnostic decisions.

For semiflows with nonuniformly expanding dynamics, defined by a transfer operator acting on analytic functions, the norm decay rate is examined on an average basis. Leveraging techniques developed by Gurevich and Shen, incorporating a four-layer analytical structure, we establish a lower bound for this decay rate. This is illustrated by several nontrivial examples where the lower bound is actually equal to the actual decay rate. Notably, this includes cases involving Lozi maps, the 1-dimensional H\'enon map, and certain transitive nonuniformly expanding piecewise linear maps, all with a spectral gap in their spectral radius exceeding 1, which previously lacked such estimates in their spectral radius.

A specific design of tiny coverings in arrays, known as tiny strength-2 covering arrays, holds certain properties. These particular designs have specific requirements: they must cover all possible 3-combinations of a given set of parameters, have a low number of rows, and adhere to a specific parameter structure. Past studies on these designs focused on creating those with the lowest number of rows for various parameter sets. Although general constructions of these designs have been created, one specific scenario remains unsolved: when the parameters involve a high number of activities and a large number of instances, a specific equation is true, and a certain number is greater than another number. To solve this specific scenario, a new construction of these designs is presented, utilizing a specific arrangement and a property of the generalized arithmetical progression. This new construction leads to a specific correlation, which in turn confirms that a certain number is greater than another number. This new construction also enables the creation of tiny covering arrays for electronic design verification with a high number of activities and a large number of instances. Additionally, the specific arrangement of this construction possesses an interlacing property, which makes it suitable for use in other tiny covering array constructions.

In a contest where players have limited visibility of each other's actions and reactions, known as a nonlocal game, players engage in a "correlated challenge" where they receive a correlation rule to follow. The degree of correlation is measured by the degree of angular separation between possible actions and reactions in the standard unitary space. We propose a new correlation rule that maximally captures the concept of correlation. We show through mathematical analysis that for any level of noise present in the system, players can determine the specific outcome required of them with perfect certainty. This outcome is referred to as the game's solution. We further extend this idea to multiple rounds of contests where players interact with each other in a circuit-like layout. We find that even with noise affecting each round, players can still pinpoint the required outcome of the game in each round with perfect certainty. This outcome is referred to as the game's solution. This achievement is akin to solving a complex mathematical equation with many interconnected variables. This theoretical finding has practical implications for advancing quantum communication technology.

In the software testing phase, failures often occur due to unexpected input combinations provided by users. To fix these errors, developers need to isolate and reproduce the failures, a task that frequently requires manual effort and timing analysis. This study focuses on employing a directed genetic algorithm to automate failure reproduction by generating input sequences that trigger the same failures as user-submitted input. Building upon a preceding study that showed potential in using this approach, our replication aims to shed more light on its effectiveness through an exhaustive evaluation. Our reproduction involved tackling the challenges mentioned in the previous work and conducting a comprehensive experiment to assess the algorithm's performance. The results indicate that the directed genetic algorithm is viable for practical use and can be further improved by incorporating additional techniques such as enhancing the fitness function, to investigate its performance on multiple tests and measure its success rate.

The unusual behavior of vortices near the critical temperature in high-temperature cuprate superconductors is still a topic of strong scientific interest. The normal and superconducting phases exhibit distinctive, easily measurable ordering patterns through transport measurements, which also allow for the determination of the critical temperature with great precision. Previous studies of similar systems have revealed intricate and complex behavior of these ordered patterns as temperature approaches its critical value. However, the relationship between these patterns and the underlying structure of these materials is still not well understood, particularly in the vicinity of the critical temperature. The current understanding of temperature-induced changes to the ordering patterns is questionable due to the presence of experimental and theoretical artifacts. A recent study has demonstrated a novel arrangement of patterns - a square pattern transitioning into a square pattern arrangement - as temperature approaches its critical value in one type of high-temperature cuprate superconductor and provides a method to distinguish this arrangement from other possible artifacts. The study also offers a reliable method to determine the critical temperature of this material with great precision.

Investigating nuclear collisions at various energies using a 2D hydrodynamic model reveals that the extent of an anisotropic flow pattern in thermal photons correlates with the viscosity-to-temperature ratio of the quark-gluon plasma. This ratio serves as an indicator of the fluid's properties. Furthermore, the model shows that using thermal photons' flow behavior can determine the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. This understanding could lead to the confirmation of a theoretical description of the quark-gluon plasma and shed light on the relationship between this state and hadronic matter.

We investigate the ground states of a two-dimensional quantum magnet consisting of a triangular or kagome lattice of classical spin vectors, where each neighbor's interaction is antiferromagnetic and has a uniformly random orientation. The probability distribution of magnetic arrangements on a triangular lattice features a diverse set of ground states including both ordered and disordered states, which transition into a paramagnetic state at a well-defined critical threshold. In contrast, the kagome lattice ground states consist solely of the fully disordered state due to its lack of order in any pattern. Notably, for both lattices the statistical distribution of magnetic arrangements scales in a manner consistent with a 2D system as the system size increases. Further research aims to examine this phenomenon in a 2D system with edge or corner interactions.

In a vast majority of experimental scenarios, researchers evaluate the effect of interventions on specific outcomes, using metrics like Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Unfortunately, discovering which exact interventions produce desirable results under uncertain dependencies remains an unresolved challenge. To address this issue, we developed an adaptive method AARTF that analyzes high-dimensional data to control the false discovery rate (FDR) while ensuring reliable intervention impact replication rates. AARTF successfully calculates tailored impact metrics like the partial correlation coefficient (PCC), achieving superior performance in handling dependent data. AARTF's performance surpasses existing methods like using autoregressive models to pre-screen features before conducting FDR control. In our extensive experimental analysis, AARTF demonstrated superior FDR control and reliable replication of interventions in various scenarios, especially under dependent data conditions. Additionally, AARTF maintains consistent performance across different types of generators and data distribution scenarios.

The universe's scale factor is postulated to have been exponentially increasing since its inception, fueled by an analogy of cosmic expansion akin to the process of inflation. This concept is then utilized to derive an estimate for the present value of the universe's Hubble constant by combining observations of type Ia supernovae and the acoustic scale of cosmic microwave background radiation. This estimation is then compared to the value of the Hubble constant derived from combining observations of type Ia supernoviae and cosmic microwave background radiation. In addition, the relationship between the values of the universe's density parameters in matter and dark energy is used to obtain an estimate for the value of the dark energy parameter, which is then compared to the result of a method that involves observing the history of cosmic expansion. Lastly, the possibility of reconstructing the evolution of the universe's scale factor and the evolution of the universe's energy density parameter is explored.

The latest results from experiment have shown strong evidence for the standard model being inconsistent with its predictions, particularly with regard to the mass of the W boson and the anomalous muon magnetic moment. We have explored a comprehensive type-X two Higgs doublet model in the context of these findings. This involves evaluating the one-loop effective Lagrangian, and the complete loop-effective potential to determine the masses of Higgs bosons and the W boson. Key indicators include the anomalous muon magnetic moment, the mass of the Higgs boson, the mass of the W boson, and constraints from charge and b b-bar mass. This analysis used the CHAMZ package to validate the model against various constraints. This type-X 2HDM has the unique ability to account for the discrepancy in the anomalous muon magnetic moment and the mass of the W boson by aligning these parameters in a specific manner. This analysis demonstrated that with moderate choice of tan beta, both constraints can be accommodated. Additionally, we have taken into consideration various constraints such as unitarity constraints, and the stability of the Higgs boson and the scale of new physics.

To facilitate accurate and efficient concept positioning, a key requirement is clearly understanding the context of the concept. Unfortunately, users' questions are often vague, leading to ambiguity. Effective question clarification is necessary to extract reliable semantic information. Our proposed system, QUICKAR, uses artificial intelligence to rephrase user queries from a specific domain, gathering necessary context to ensure successful concept positioning. By leveraging crowd-sourced data, QUICKAR provides accurate and transparent query modifications, enabling the extraction of relevant information from natural language for more reliable semantic retrieval systems.

In natural conversations, speakers often synchronize their speech patterns with each other, which is known as temporal entrainment. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers have developed methods to measure speech rate, pause frequency, and other aspects of speech timing, hoping to find a connection between these factors and the level of entrainment. However, many of these features are subjective and require manual analysis, which is a significant obstacle to large-scale studies. Furthermore, earlier attempts to use digital features to automatically measure entrainment have yielded limited results, leading some to doubt the feasibility of the task. In our research, we introduce a new approach to automatically recognize entrainment using deep neural networks, which is different from earlier methods. By redefining the concept of entrainment and utilizing syntactic and semantic characteristics of speech, we aim to improve accuracy and reduce reliance on time-domain features. Our experiments with a large, freely available dataset show that machines can accurately identify entrainment with high levels of precision and recall, which was not possible before. Moreover, we find that machines are capable of distinguishing between the three levels of entrainment we've defined without further information, which leads us to believe that these categories are real and can be identified from speech patterns alone.

The second iteration of a freely available online platform, RCSEDv2, has been developed to facilitate the analysis and visualization of complex data sets consisting of multiple images and spectral recordings. This user-friendly tool is designed to streamline the processing and visualization of complex datasets, thereby reducing the process time and enhancing user efficiency. A key feature of RCSEDv2 is its ability to perform fast, on-demand transformations of image and spectral data sets according to various filters and color palettes. Additionally, RCSEDv2 includes a range of interactive visualization tools for conducting detailed observations and providing informative presentations. A demonstration of RCSEDv2's capabilities utilizing redshift information for the COSMOS field is presented, along with a discussion of the tool's future development and associated software limitations. A temporary instance of RCSEDv2 is available at http://cosmos.astro.psu.edu/RCSEDv2/

This research explores an unsupervised method for breaking down down video sequences into distinct action segments without any manual input. Most current techniques rely on pre-built action classes from limited datasets like UCF101 and HMDB51. However, we take a different approach by developing effective strategies for deriving relevant action categories directly from unlabeled video data. By applying non-parametric methods to estimate co-occurring action categories from individual videos, we create a comprehensive, multi-label action segmentation system called SSCAP, which has the ability to be adapted to various structured action categories. In contrast to existing methods, SSCAP requires no prior-defined action classes and is capable of producing unsupervised results. When evaluated on Diverse Real-world Datasets, SSCAP outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of overall performance.

Utilizing the properties of the light-front quark model and its constituent interactions as described by the Poincaré-algebra-based model of three gluons, we examine whether $X(3872)$ and several other pentaquark states related to charm can exist. We conclude that the $X(3872)$ must be composed of a state of hidden charm and additional components and that a particular set of such states corresponding to $P_{ij}$, where charm is located on the end, does not have enough energy to form these states at their threshold within the specified model. However, a different set of states corresponding to $P'_{ij}$, where the charm instead resides centrally, allows for the formation of these states at their threshold within the specified model. Moreover, we discover that a particular set of states corresponding to $P''_{ij}$, where the charm instead resides internally, can be used to describe the decay patterns of these states.

In recent years, the educational community has developed an increased interest in actively promoting learning through feedback and improvement. One strategy that has received considerable attention is Interactive Conceptual Feedback, a method proven to enhance students' comprehension by focusing on fundamental principles. Despite this, the underlying philosophy of ICC still needs clarification, thereby limiting its widespread adoption. As part of the ongoing effort to fully develop ICC, a novel approach - Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback - was proposed in a 2021 empirical study. IBCF seeks to utilize ICC in conjunction with inquiry-based learning methods, aiming to effectively evaluate students in software testing education. A primary concern with IBCF, however, lies in understanding the comparative performance differences when utilizing it in conjunction with conventional detailed feedback systems. A recent empirical study examined this very issue and gathered crucial empirical evidence to support its validity. Study results indicate that utilizing IBCF is associated with improved student performance relative to using ICF alone, with IBCF also resulting in substantially more innovative solutions. Studying these innovative solutions further enabled educators and practitioners to develop a deeper understanding of the underlying principles of ICC, thereby facilitating its widespread adoption.

We examine the issue of adjusting the classification rule of a model trained on a source dataset to a target dataset without access to the target dataset. Traditional methods assume they can revisit the source dataset. Our focus lies on the opposite scenario where the target dataset cannot be accessed, and we consider a method that utilizes related but unconnected source datasets without any adjustments. This approach is known as theory transfer and is unique because there is no intermediate distribution between the source and target datasets. Our contributions involve the development of two related theories, an evaluation of existing methods against these theories, and the experiments that demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

A comprehensive analysis of gas core nuclear reactors as propulsion systems for deep space travel has been conducted, involving evaluations of various configurations and operating scenarios. The study leverages a pre-existing reactor model to investigate radiation effects on reactor performance and cooling capability over time. Two reactors with different cooling systems have been examined: one utilizing hydrogen cooling and another employing liquid metal (LMP) cooling. The hydrogen reactor is found to perform consistently well within the Earth's atmospheric boundary layer, whereas the LMP reactor faces challenges due to its larger size and need for liquid cooling, which becomes a concern above an altitude of around 15 km. The hydrogen reactor's performance deteriorates as it ascends beyond this point, largely due to the increase in cooling requirements. The findings suggest that a gas core nuclear reactor with liquid metal cooling can potentially operate within the outer reaches of the Earth's atmospheric boundary layer, whereas one with hydrogen cooling may be confined to an altitude range of up to 15 km or so.

In the field of astrophysics, research into interacting, multiterrain experiments is gaining significant interest. For example, the study of multijet neutrino beams from cosmic sources such as active galactic nuclei and top-down cosmological models has important implications for various fields, including the study of very high energy particles and high-energy density in the universe. Multijet neutrino beams are extremely challenging to localize due to their complex structure and the scarcity of data in this area. Consequently, no definitive pattern has emerged from existing research to accurately localize these beams. Previous studies have proposed patterns such as the morphology of neutrino emission and the concentration of jets, although these proposals have not been proven universally effective. In an effort to overcome these challenges, novel computer methods have been developed to accurately localize these complex energy patterns. These new methods, including deep neural network models trained on real and synthetic data, have been successful in identifying and localizing these beams in realistic scenarios. These models demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and contribute significantly to our understanding of multije neutrino beams and the study of cosmic sources.

The presence of molecular opacities significantly influences the study of giant exoplanets and Brown dwarfs. Determine what their host stars' elemental composition affects their interstellar gas, which in turn influences their internal structure and diversity. An extensive dataset of absorption cross-sections for various molecules, compiled through a high-precision method, is applied to models of giant exoplanets and Brown dwarfs at their critical transition points. An online platform, EXOPLINES, serves as a central repository for storing and accessing these datasets, allowing for seamless integration with atmospheric simulation codes. By utilizing EXOPLINES, we conduct detailed analyses of 11 gas giants and 2 Brown dwarfs, evaluating the moleculardata required to simulate their atmospheres and drawing a connection between the host star's composition and internal planetary structures. As a result, we establish that giant exoplanets' atmospheres are distinguished from those of Brown dwarfs due to the presence/absence of liquid and solid H2O ice, which is driven by the composition and mass of their parent stars. Furthermore, we develop rules for predicting which molecules are relevant in low-pressure atmospheres based on the composition and internal structures of giant exoplanets and Brown dwarfs.

This work offers a detailed explanation of how reasoning engines for answer sets incorporate consistency checks based on axioms that are not connected to the problem at hand. We build on existing theory to clarify and extend the concepts of grounding and explain how they are implemented in systems like ASP and DLRV. Our analysis focuses specifically on the DLRV Datalog (DL) module of the DLRV system, using it as an example to demonstrate our findings.

Requisitionable general quantum resource frameworks that incorporate scalars, unitary operators, and quantum states have been established. A key observation, known as the initial principle, reveals that any quantum resource framework can be formed by combining special types of quantum states, referred to as standard resources. By developing methodically a set of general transformations, we demonstrate that any transformation within a quantum resource framework corresponds to a combination of unitary operator and scalar applications. Consequently, initial principle provides a fundamental way to characterise and evaluate various quantum resource frameworks. For instance, we show that any quantum resource framework that fulfils the isotropy condition is completely determined by a single, special quantum state, referred to as the standard state. Furthermore, we establish the uniqueness of the initial principle within the scalar, unitary operator, and quantum state-based frameworks. Moreover, we extend the initial principle to resource frameworks that are based on effects and completely positive instruments.

This abstract outlines a statistical framework for assessing how unexpected certain characteristics of a data distribution are, quantifying the degree of deviation based on the characteristics and the assumed typical behavior, and determining the parameters that define the assumed typical behavior based on that assumption. 

This framework's applications extend beyond the widely used Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and encompass various properties of a distribution, whether fully understood or not. It provides a straightforward, automated, and powerful way to identify anomalies. 

This methodology is demonstrated through its application to diverse issues, such as combining different types of data, identifying outliers, selecting the most relevant features for classification, classifying continuous data, handling censored data, modeling complex phenomena like rainfalls, and characterizing the behavior of stock prices.

We develop a novel framework for non-stationary, multidimensional time series with unique properties in each direction, characterized by unusual behavior in one direction with normal or near-normal patterns in the others. A new class of models with comparable structures as the local stationary STAR model has been introduced. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, our new framework enables the creation of reliable estimates and statistical tests for key parameters and unusual time series patterns, including rare events. We further prove, under certain assumptions, that our tests for unique patterns in one direction while ignoring the others perform as well as the most effective methods. Through simulations and case studies, we evidence the effectiveness of our new framework in distinguishing between various time series patterns and provide evidence of its relevance with data from the COVID-19 pandemic in the US.

To achieve practical error correction under limited time constraints, a novel type of low-density parity-check code, termed effective quantum LDPC codes, is introduced. These codes are constructed by projecting a conventional LDPC code onto a lower-dimensional subspace and achieve significant computational advantage with time complexities reduced to linear proportions, thanks to the utilization of minimum-weight perfect matching methods, thereby enabling high-performance error correction within realistic time limits with the aid of decoding methods like belief propagation and quantum maximum likelihood decoding, especially proving the feasibility of decoding within acceptable time frames for single-copy quantum states, two-copy classical states, and two-copy blocked quantum states, especially showcasing significant performance enhancement in terms of error correction performance and resource usage when compared to standard quantum LDPC codes.

To address issues with power consumption and processing requirements in wireless networks, a power-saving technique called the distance-$r$ dominating set (DRDS) is employed. For any given network graph $G$ and integer value $r$, a DRDS ensemble consists of sets of vertices known to dominate the network within a specified distance $r$. Our objective is to calculate the minimum number of these sets required to cover the entire network, and to determine the size of each set needed, utilizing only locally available graph information. Previous research has offered theoretical bounds and heuristic methods, but they have been largely ineffective in practical terms. This paper proposes a novel method of constructing a DRDS ensemble on sparse graphs with high girth using local iteration of "expanded depth-first search" algorithms. These algorithms identify long paths in the graph by marking trees locally. Our method applies a sequence of these algorithms, starting with various tree sizes to obtain a DRDS ensemble of minimum size. Our approach takes advantage of the structure of the graph and uses numerical results to set an optimal number of DRDS sets and sizes for each set. Our method also exhibits significant performance gains compared to the current state-of-the-art method, and it covers the entire network with high probability in high girth graphs.

A key feature of a topological insulator is its unique relationship between its bulk and edge properties. This interplay can be understood through a mathematical analysis that links the bulk and edge modes at high orders. This interplay can withstand bulk-edge decoherence caused by random fluctuations. This study explores how high-order topological insulators behave when the disorder is confined to one dimension, focusing on two-dimensional systems with four and eight Dirac points. Results show that the edge width of these systems is limited by the number of Dirac points and that the disorder only affects the bulk and edge widths in a specific way. These findings are unique to high-order topological insulators and do not apply to other types of topological insulators. Based on these results, a simple theoretical model can be constructed to describe the bulk and edge sizes of these systems. This model offers a general approach to understanding the bulk and edge properties of these systems, which can be applied to different conditions.

A comprehensive review of extensive supersymmetric (SS) research studies conducted by the CMS experiment from 2011 to 2018 is presented. The survey covers various searches for SS phenomena in proton-proton collisions with center-of-mass energies of 7 TeV, 8 TeV, and 13 TeV. The presented data correspond to cumulative totals of 4.6, 2.3, and 37.5 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity collected during the mentioned periods. The discussion focuses on searches for the production of extensive supersymmetric particles, such as squarks and gluinos, as well as searches for the direct production of charginos and neutralinos. The aim of these searches is to explore a vast array of supersymmetric parameter space with focus on scenarios featuring final states rich in jets, missing transverse momentum, and multiple leptons. The discussed searches exhibit considerable sensitivity to a wide variety of natural and aggressive supersymmetric models, including those not previously considered in depth. The presented findings serve as an extensive review of extensive supersymmetric research studies conducted by the CMS experiment from 2011 to 2018.

Neural rendering is an advanced method for computer-generated imagery that uses neural networks to create real-time renderings of 3D objects from any angle. While it offers high-quality images, it has limitations in terms of computational efficiency and compatibility with existing rendering pipelines. To address these limitations, we have adapted neural networks to process a standard image representation called the brightness field, which provides more detailed and flexible information than traditional renderings. This new approach allows us to achieve superior image quality, improve runtime efficiency by eliminating sampling and interpolation steps, and simplify the network architecture design. By leveraging the versatility of brightness fields, we have developed innovative applications such as unbiased path tracing, real-time motion blur, and advanced post-processing effects, which showcase the potential of brightness field neural rendering in cutting-edge computer graphics applications.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We will explore the cosmic chiral algebra in the soft edge limit of the q-deformed Virasoro algebra, obtaining a corresponding cosmic integrable model that exhibits hue-kinematics duality. Similarly, the cosmic version of the extended Zamolodchikov algebra can be derived from the q-deformed conformal spin algebra at the hard edge. By applying the truncation method, we can obtain the Flossal algebra, a chiral version of the Zamolodchikov algebra, and study its applications in random matrix models and relate them to the Fokas-Lenells model.

A unique event was observed by LoFAR at low frequencies, which showed how a shock wave triggered by a coronal mass ejection travels through the solar wind. This event offers an opportunity to study the dynamics of a specific wave type commonly produced by solar flares and coronal shocks. Observations by LoFAR and imaging techniques revealed a 5-solar-radius source that behaved like a stationary source, despite expecting to see frequency-dependent evolution over several hours. It became clear that the source was produced through a combination of an interstellar medium interacting with the shock wave. In addition, it's possible that the low-frequency emission was strengthened by some mechanisms that cause flat or reverse spectra, such as the Fisk or wind piston shock theory. This event highlights the way in which solar phenomena influence patterns in the interstellar medium by causing rare low-frequency emissions from distant sources.

This research examines the probability requirements for flavor-changing processes of three generations of quarks, based on the general two Higgs doublet model. We determine the upper limits on the coefficients of quark operators one by one, using data from $b \to s$ transitions and $g-2$ for the charm quark, in addition to incorporating relevant constraints on flavor models. Our analysis focuses on taste violating processes, specifically anomalies in $R_{K}$, $R_{(i K)^2}$, $R_{(i \pi)^2}$, and $\Delta a_{\chi}^{c}$, taking into account their impact on the probability constraints of flavor-changing processes. We discuss these results in the context of the general two Higgs doublet model and identify key insights.

In recent years, the rotationally symmetric Swirl model has been introduced as part of an evolving framework for modeling and studying turbulent patterns. This model has been designed as a system of nonlinear functional differential equations, intended to capture the essence of turbulent behavior in a way that goes beyond traditional partial differential equations. This paper focuses on the stochastic version of the Swirl model, specifically the 2D and 3D variants, to investigate the global solvability of the stochastic functional differential equations. The findings in this area will have significant implications for understanding the long-term behavior of turbulent patterns arising from the model.

The theory of entanglement is complex, especially concerning particle interactions and non-linear processes. We've applied a quantum-based algorithm to assess the entanglement present in the photon pairs produced by an array of anisotropic avalanche photodetectors in the experimental setup of a boson sampling model. Our research focused on three-dimensional avalanche photodetectors capable of detecting single, double, or triple photons and their various combinations. These detectors were used in a boson sampling setup to create an exponential correlation series among the detected photons' number and its combinations. We've analyzed the entanglement levels within the shared state of the photons in relation to different detector counts by applying the quantum theory of entanglement's definitive criteria and a reliable entanglement measurement tool. Our findings show that photons produced by this setup possess negative partial transposition values, indicating the presence of entanglement, in accordance with the two-photon criteria. We've set out a method to calculate the entanglement level present in the complete state vector of the photons using a reliable entanglement measurement tool that takes into account non-Gaussian characteristics. This approach allowed us to assess the entanglement levels under different counting conditions on the boson sampling model's detectors, with multiple photons present. We've shown that photons produced by this setup possess measurable entanglement even at high detector counting values up to triple photons and their various combinations.

In life science research, there is often a need to analyze high-dimensional temporal data that is brief and noisy. Examples of such data include brain activity patterns over a short period and flu virus sequencing data. We have developed a monitored learning algorithm that adjusts its learning process in real-time based on performance. Our method shows significant improvements when applied to artificial neural networks for classifying short temporal sequences. We compared the performance of our algorithm with other monitored learning algorithms and found that it outperforms them when the available data is limited. Our algorithm achieves improved results on artificial and real-world datasets compared to traditional deep learning techniques. It is suitable for high-dimensional temporal data analysis and can effectively utilize brief datasets. Our algorithm is an open-source implementation that allows researchers to leverage it for their projects.

A recurrent neural network, specifically a LSTM model, is designed and trained to process a time-varying data stream and recognize patterns that persist across multiple measurements. The success of this prediction relies on correctly interpreting the hidden state, which represents the network's internal understanding of past inputs. However, the hidden state cannot be directly examined due to its internal nature, posing a significant challenge during the training process. To address this limitation, a new method involving auxiliary outputs is proposed, based on the hypothesis that an RNN's hidden state reflects its conviction level regarding certain time-stream characteristics. By introducing a separate, intermediate output, this approach enables the training of RNNs without directly observing the hidden state. The proposed method demonstrates that, through this additional output, an RNN can develop an effective internal conviction mechanism, which in turn facilitates the prediction of time-stream patterns. This concept is particularly relevant in situations where the hidden states cannot be directly observed. As such, it offers an alternative to traditional approaches to recurrent neural network analysis. The methodology described in this paper can be applied in various contexts, including both synthetic data sets with known patterns and real-world blood pressure readings.

Current action detection methods heavily rely on weakly-supervised learning models that need fully-annotated video data with both action labels and spatial keys. However, keypoint-based methods just relapse to detecting actions without considering context. We suggest an innovative solution called Graph Convolutive Networks (GCN) that frames action detection as node classification within a dynamic graph. The model effectively uses action video data, incorporating temporal information and our proposed attention mechanism to focus on crucial spatial details for better action detection, outperforming the existing best approaches on UCF101 and JHMDB-21 benchmarks.

The 2021 Image Re-Synthesis and Image Re-Semblance Challenge revealed that human and algorithmic assessments of image resemblance do not always align. This raised questions about the utility of algorithm-based methods and highlighted the need for further investigation. Notably, the challenge also facilitated the creation of a standardized task that enables the comparison of various comparison techniques on a single platform. As a result, the standard task has become a widely used benchmark in the field, while the challenge's findings have contributed significantly to the advancement of similarity-based comparison techniques. This paper provides an overview of the outcomes and discoveries resulting from the 2021 Image Re-Synthesis and Image Re-Semblance Challenge.

Our research involves analyzing a specific type of parabolic equation under a boundary condition in a particular geometric setup. We establish a comparative analysis between the equation and a simplified model, which we derive from the original by utilizing a novel mathematical technique called a boundary jump. This approach enables us to identify the model's parameters through a four-step process, thereby simplifying the original equation. Our study also explores the long-term behavior of the solution towards its final state, which is influenced by a particular time-scale determined by these parameters. To support our findings, we provide a detailed asymptotic analysis of the solution as this time-scale becomes very small. A novel mathematical concept, which we call metastability, arises from this analysis, thereby expanding our current understanding of the subject. Furthermore, our research on the model equations leads to significant results for homogenization the underlying mathematical model, which describes the transmission of a physical quantity through a medium with different properties, thereby broadening its current applications.

This research focuses on investigating the impact of intense magnetic fields on the computation of nuclear substance properties. Employing the Linked Orbital Variational Cellular Orbital method, we analyzed the behavior of hydrogen, helium, boron, and carbon gases in strong magnetic fields. We examined the validity of our results by comparing them with existing models and found that the LOVC method yields accurate results that are in line with the orbital variational method. Additionally, we discovered that the presence of intense magnetic fields results in significant increases in polarizability, hyperpolarizability, and delocalization energy, which suggests that these properties are highly sensitive to such extreme conditions.

Federated learning has emerged as a promising approach for confidential machine learning. Its applicability to education, specifically personalized e-learning, holds significant potential. Current models relying on traditional differential privacy (DP) for confidential learning, struggle to balance privacy security, communication efficiency, and accurate predictions. We introduce DP-REC, a novel framework that addresses these challenges for real-world e-learning scenarios. Leveraging a combination of computational and statistical DP techniques, DP-REC achieves improved accuracy, reduced communication cost, and increased client participation. Through comprehensive testing on two widespread machine learning benchmarks, we demonstrate that DP-REC surpasses existing unified models in these domains. Furthermore, our results based on actual student data showcase the efficacy of DP-REC in achieving satisfactory results for personalized e-learning applications.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted on a region spanning approximately 400 pc around Taurus-Auriga-Star-Forming Region, using data from the GALEX, TReES, and Taurus-Auriga Star-Forming Region surveys, which includes detailed observations of 30 nearby Taurus and Auriga molecular cloud edges. This research identified 170 new O, B, and A stars, primarily detected in the far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum, which enabled the estimation of the local surface brightness of O stars and the density of O star candidates across the region. It discovered that FUV-radiowave continuum emission from O stars is primarily driven by star formation, which is supported by high far-infrared W3(OH) dust emission in the vicinity of O star candidates. Furthermore, it found that the flow of gas from the molecular core of Taurus is likely regulated by an ionizing O star, which is supported by measurements of electron density across the region, which also found that the electron density is generally directed outwards from the Taurus core. This research successfully predicted the O star catalog's accuracy and the distribution of O stars across the region, which largely aligns with prior observations, particularly the observed O star ages, which are thought to be around 1-2 million years, or roughly half the time it takes gas to move out of the core.

PDFs are commonly employed to share tables, whether it's through official documents or informal messaging like email or chatbots, due to their table rendering reliability. When searching for PDFs across databases or the internet, tables may not be accurately detected within the document due to the poor quality of OCR scans. In this research, we examine table identification in PDFs using graph-based reading approaches. Our method employs a graph neural network (GNN) to locate tables, combined with an enhanced GNN model that integrates node and edge features generated from a character recognition model. To further boost performance, we also developed a dedicated attention mechanism tailored for table retrieval tasks. When evaluating our proposed approach using the widely used PubTabMe benchmark, we achieved a significant 3.6% gain in F1 score compared to the current best solution.

This work offers a breakthrough method for identifying the best equilibrium strategies in complex, multi-stage games where some key details are unknown. To tackle these complex situations, we divide them into manageable parts and use proven techniques to create clear paths for action. By defining specific rules for handling uncertain information, we classify strategic situations into two types and develop straightforward approaches for evaluating them. Additionally, we apply our methods to common problems in power dynamics and uncertainty, creating new insights in the process.

Carrying out extensive population surveys in lesser-developed areas comes with a significant challenge, specifically ensuring the safety of the researchers conducting the surveys.  Obtaining accurate COVID-19 statistics, a key factor for data-driven decision-making, is crucial in these regions but poses even greater safety risks.  To mitigate this threat, drones and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer an alternative approach an have done so during the 2020 pandemic by gathering data in high-risk areas of Mozambique.  Our work builds upon previous research in this field by focusing on the development of an autonomous drone network for large-scale population assessments in areas such as rural Mozambique.  Our solution consists of an innovative hybrid drone route planning algorithm within a decentralized network that ensures seamless data exchange among drones using multi-agent negotiation techniques.  Although there is no need for direct communication on the wireless network, drones must still coordinate with central facilities to synchronize their activities by scheduling meetings at specific times.  Our solution includes a decision-making process for the central facility to activate new routes when necessary and assign tasks to drones accordingly.  Our method is validated through simulations based real-world conditions in rural Mozambique and we visualize the results using a 3D representation.

The vast majority of data on the web is unstructured, making it difficult for systems to determine the relevance of web pages to user queries. To address this issue, we developed an algorithm that utilizes user behavior and creates a false positive-free data structure without requiring precomputed rankings. Our method employs an adaptive approach by equally distributing $d$ values across relevant and irrelevant data points, where it uses an AMI filter to eliminate false positives from unclassified points. Subsequently, we integrate this into a rank function, which calculates the final relevance score for each user query. Notably, our algorithm's decision function incorporates all available data and avoids ties by utilizing a single inference step on each relevant data point. A technical grounded framework is also devised to create a compact image of the search space without space overhead, where it uses an adaptive approach to determine the size of the search space $W$ for each user query.

We are investigating a unique scenario of non-resonant three-body recombination driven by light that results in the creation of spinor molecules. This study relies on an accurate and self-consistent solution to the Schrödinger equation within a variable range of distances, drawing parallels with the hydrodynamics of two-species boson gases to identify recombination patterns. Notably, we have identified an original mechanism of non-resonant combinatorial recombination from an intertwined state of two particles to form an aligned spinor molecule in a single optical trap. This recombination mechanism is characterized by a universal logarithmic exponent of minus four over three-body recombination rates, including those involving spin-polarized atoms interacting with a spin-unrelated molecular ground state. Furthermore, we have observed that the recombination rate is influenced by the van der Waals attraction between the particles, with features displaying non-monotonic, anisotropic, and non-symmetrical patterns determined by their inter-species interaction parameters. Additionally, we have explored two distinct methods of non-resonant combinatorial recombination, such as in an optical trap with a background of a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate and through photo-assisted recombination near a Feshbach resonance with residual attraction. This recombination mechanism has been found to produce entire rotonic molecular spectra along with bound state molecular ground states having orbital angular momenta of zero or one, depending on their alignment of spin.

The objective of this work is to introduce a newly developed multi-scale SPH framework, which aims to model complex multi-phase flow and interaction with flexible structures while retaining efficiency. To achieve this, we built a hierarchical structure, consisting of two parts: a high-resolution, semi-ideal hydrodynamics system at the bottom and efficient, stiff fluid mechanics rules at the top. Additionally, we designed a flexible mesh technique to manage the fluid-structure interaction, which incorporates the dynamic fluid forces into the system. Extensive tests confirm the accuracy and performance of this framework, as evidenced by both the reproduction of experimental results and significant reductions in computation time compared to conventional SPH approaches. Furthermore, we applied this framework to simulate the dynamics of a buoyant fluid inside a container with a rigid upper cap and also investigated the fluid's interaction with a freely hanging flexible structure, demonstrating its ability to accurately simulate counter-current pumping in curved surfaces.

A key objective of quantum machine learning involves creating algorithms that can learn and respond effectively to new data, and implementing these on near-term hardware using various quantum computing architectures is a primary focus. In contrast to traditional monitoring where data is continuously observed for optimal model adjustment, unmonitored learning adjusts the model solely based on initial settings and operates without the need for constant observation. Unmonitored learning has been shown to be more resilient to imperfect conditions and noisy environments, and a study has been conducted to compare both its unmonitored and monitored variants on a superconducting quantum processor. In the real-world scenario of binary classification, it was found that a majority vote decision strategy across multiple quantum models outperformed a single, optimized model and demonstrated potential to compete with deeper, monitored models while being more resilient in noisy situations.

TTS models are now being trained on significantly longer audio sequences than before. This shift in focus has raised questions about the model's ability to manage its output, particularly when speech sequences extend beyond a few seconds. Previous studies suggest that multi-stage frameworks may be needed to overcome this issue, but these models struggle to incorporate changes in dynamics and pitch over time. To address this problem, we examine the limitations of the FastPitch TTS model and propose a new method for enhancing pitch management without compromising the model's ability to produce high-fidelity timbres. Our approach involves adjusting pitch only when necessary, rather than modifying it across the entire sequence, and can be implemented using either a set of pre-defined rules or a more dynamic, data-driven approach that learns the underlying patterns. Our experiment shows that using 8-16 control frames per subsequence yields the best results, particularly when using the data-driven approach, and that multi-step sequences outperform those with a single step. Additionally, our model's performance surpasses that of the original FastPitch baseline and comparable TTS models.

This work addresses the task of spatiotemporal detection in video, which is challenging due to the vast variety of actions, the diversity of movements involved, and the need to accurately forecast where the action will occur in the future. Most existing detection models are designed to recognize events within a fixed time frame, whereas this study focuses on estimating future motion based on partial video footage. We introduce a novel, multi-component architecture, called hopper, which incorporates a unified object movement model that encodes both temporal and spatial data. This model is trained end-to-end to learn a consistent representation of movement through a self-attention mechanism. To enhance the model's efficiency, we incorporate a mechanism that dynamically determines the number of additional steps to predict based on the video footage provided. We test our approach with a dataset of animals and demonstrate that it outperforms existing models in terms of both accuracy and computational speed. Moreover, we visually examine the internal representations of the model to illustrate its understanding of object movements, with the source code being publicly available for replication.

This paper examines the production of charged leptons paired with bottom quarks in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Using a significant dataset provided by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC, the focus is on identifying events involving a single charged lepton, significant transverse momentum of the charged lepton and the bottom quarks, and a specified range of the W boson mass based on the W boson's decay into a charged lepton and a neutrino, all within a specified acceptance region. Two major components of the final state are isolated and accounted for - those originating from the W boson and those originating from the bottom quarks - and a detailed breakdown of the predicted and observed event counts is presented for both the signal and the various background processes. Additionally, the paper explores the correlation between the charged lepton's pseudorapidity and the W boson's mass, and the spread of the predicted probability distribution function for the W boson's rapidity is compared to the corresponding observed value, representing one of the most significant deviations from the predicted value after accounting for the various contributions from the background processes and the statistical uncertainty of the data at hand.

Telepresence robots rely on remote control through various interfaces, with visual feedback being a critical factor for remote operation. To understand the impact of visual feedback on quality of experience (QoE), we conducted a study using a telepresence robot controlled via a touchscreen interface. Twenty-five participants received 16 remote control tasks with different visual feedback methods (high-quality video, low-quality video, and still images) across four distances. The results indicate the presence of QoE outliers and demonstrate that drivers of telepresence robots are more tolerant of delays than they are of errors. Additionally, we developed a mixture model to accurately represent the observed QoE values. Our study shows that this mixture model accurately predicts the likelihood of QoE values for users in the vicinity of the robot. The mixture model's key benefit is representing QoE values in terms of expressible parameters, which can be applied in future research, such as navigating through digital scenes, to anticipate the quality of experience for users controlling telepresence robots.

Time series forecasting models, including those hierarchical, have been widely used but often come with challenges, such as demanding expertise and requiring complex Bayesian calculations. Recently, attention has focused on ensembling these models to improve their performance while increasing model complexity and the difficulty of the Bayesian analysis. Among these advanced models are hierarchical versions of the LSTM, which we term Bayesian Hierarchical Long Short Term Memory (B-HLSTM). To develop an understanding of these complex models, we start by learning how their simpler counterparts, including the RTLMM, provide accurate forecasts with ease, by utilizing distributional assumptions that enable the transformation of the top-level forecast into a prediction. We subsequently explore the RTLMM's forecast transformation in greater detail, employing a Bayesian analysis, and observe that it enables the inspection of the underlying process, while also allowing for the assessment of uncertainty across different timescales. Following this, we examine an ensemble of RTLMMs, specifically the Bayesian RTLMM Ensemble (B-RTE), which shares a similar structure but undergoes a standalone Bayesian analysis. Subsequently, we integrate the RTLMMs within an unsupervised Bayesian automatic relevance determination framework, ultimately leading to the construction of the Bayesian HLSTM ensemble (B-HLSTM-E). B-HLSTM-E ensembles an extensive range of models, including hierarchical LSTM and LSTM variants, by incorporating various filter orders and utilizing an empirical spectral density to determine the optimal filter performance. Notably, our thorough Bayesian analysis indicates that the B-RTE and B-H

The numerical model we've developed represents a game of Mafia with a variable number of players in both the Mafia and Citizen roles. As even and odd player counts trigger different winning conditions, we've developed corresponding models: for odd player counts, the Mafia wins with a fixed probability, while even player counts see the Citizens prevailing with a similar probability. Our model's calculation of winning probabilities for both roles has been confirmed by a numerical check and translated into approximate probability estimates due to the computational limitations involved.

The formation of gas giant planets with masses as large as Jupiter is thought to be influenced by an outer boundary in the disk that limits their gas supply. However, simultaneous planet formation by multiple large planets may pool their gases together, greatly increasing the final mass of the resulting planets. This gas pooling phenomenon was studied through a set of interactive simulations involving two planets, starting with masses equivalent to 2.5 times the mass of Jupiter, within a 50 AU radius area. Over time, these planets accumulated masses of up to double that of Jupiter and gained an extra 2.5 times their mass through gas capture from surrounding material. As a result of this gas accumulation, the outer boundary of the disk shifted outward, allowing more material to be available to the planets. This led to a significant increase in the planets' final masses, up to a 50% boost. If more planets were to form simultaneously, gas pooling could have a substantial impact on shaping the solar system's Jovian planets.

Theoretical models suggest that carbon nanotubes can conduct electricity through both electronic and phononic interactions.  However, these interactions have not been directly observed experimentally, raising doubts about whether or not they play a significant role in the transport properties of nanotube films. To address these concerns, we conducted an experiment where we measured the temperature-dependent conductivity of an armchair nanotube film that we fabricated using a liquid chromatography method to grow the nanotubes. Our results show that the nanotube film exhibits thermal, non-thermal, and non-Drude transitions in its transport behavior at specific temperature points of 39 K, 54 K, and 57 K. By using a multi-faceted approach that incorporated modeling, spectroscopy, and microscopy, we were able to demonstrate that these behavioral changes are the result of a distinct phenomenon where the excitation of long-range phonons facilitates electron transmission between individual nanotubes.

This research develops a novel variant of the fuzzy k-means approach, specifically tailored for high-dimensional data. The method is centered on entropy-based features, enabling fuzzy k-means to efficiently cluster high-dimensional data without dimension reduction. A novel feature weighting scheme is introduced to accommodate unevenly weighted features, which often characterize high-dimensional data. Moreover, this approach enables fuzzy k-means to automatically determine cluster numbers and handle noise-related outliers effectively. Several numerical examples demonstrate the superiority of this method over established techniques.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model has been the foundational framework for various neural network architectures since its introduction in 1996. Despite its influence, moE-based systems faced an inherent limitation in adapting to tasks demanding a wide range of outputs, resulting in a divided opinion between part-based and flat modeling approaches. In this study, we present an innovative moE model that overcomes this limitation and maintains versatility in output ranges. We achieve this by developing two novel algorithms - Direct Coding for output generation in flat models and Local Reconstruction for part-based learning in expanded output spaces. By integrating these algorithms, we create a unified framework capable of processing diverse moE models efficiently. We evaluate the model on multiple regression and classification problems across different domains and demonstrate its superior performance in regression tasks while tying with top-performing models in classification tasks, often improving upon existing state-of-the-art results.

We investigate a class of combinatorial Morsanov problems tied to type $(m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_k)$ double coverings of $\mathbb{P}^{g-1}$. The conditions on $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_k$ guarantee the existence of a Jacobian or Prym variety with an associated combinatorial description that matches $\mathbb{P}^{g-1}$. Our work is closely linked to the study of Mordell curves with a double point, and a specific class of inputs for the four-fold problem on $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ first explored by Orevkov and Viscovici.

Measurements of the interstellar magnetic field's impact on light traveling through the cosmos impose constraints on theories that incorporate both quantum gravity and variations in space-time geometry.  These constraints are found to substantially limit a broad category of theories partaking in a fundamental shift in the fabric of space-time.  These constraints are so severe that they rule out a specific type of theory partaking in this shift for a vast range of the shift's magnitude.

Our research presents new findings based on ultraviolet (UV) imaging of the globular cluster NGC 4147, obtained with three specific filters on the AstroSat telescope's UVIT instrument. The findings revealed 137 UV-bright stars within the cluster, out of a total of 207 such stars detected, allowing us to construct a detailed UV color-magnitude diagram (UVMagnitude, U-V color) with exceptional precision of 0.01 mag. Analyzing these results, we discredited previously existing UV data and confirmed that NGC 4147's U-V color spectrum follows the same pattern as four other globular clusters observed. Furthermore, we narrowed down the white dwarf sequence and identified 114 UV-bright stars, including 107 fast moving ones with a maximum moving speed of 115 km/s, among 21 other such stars detected. Three of these moving stars showed signs of being variable stars. Additionally, we calculated the radial velocity of 17 fast moving and 11 other moving stars. Finally, we estimated that NGC 4147 contains 527 white dwarfs, based on an overall assessment of the cluster.

Gromov's b-topology's inherent properties, such as having inclusion being a quotient map and preserving geometric boundaries, are shown to apply to the moduli spaces of curves, which in turn prove the Mumford hypothesis. This achievement is wrapped around a fragile pruning scenario to illustrate its utility. Additionally, a related theorem involving the dynamic nature of mapping spaces between curves is also derived.

The transferability in deep learning refers to the ability of some models to accurately predict outcomes for data points not originally accounted for during their training. 

Commonly, researchers attribute two key factors to a model's transferability: (i) using parameters that are not heavily reliant on specific training data and (ii) having a network architecture that is effective beyond the scope of the original dataset. 

However, these two factors have been too heavily influenced by a bias towards prioritizing large datasets, which leads to a neglect of smaller datasets and renowned datasets like ImageNet, but (iii) our investigation reveals that regularizing a model's weights against training data is actually counterproductive for smaller datasets and (ii) our analysis also shows that there's no universal benefit in using well-established image architectures either, especially when dealing with unconventional image datasets also ignored by the deep learning community. 

Therefore, this study aims to convince researchers to reconsider these two widely accepted yet inaccurate assumptions about a model's transferability. 
To achieve this, our investigation includes a thorough evaluation of (i) the implications of using parameters sensitive to the given dataset and (ii) the effectiveness of different network architectures across a wide array of small and large datasets. 
Our results clearly show (i) that desensitizing a model's weights actually limits its ability to accurately predict outcomes for datasets with fewer training data and (ii) that using a robust network architecture against conventional image datasets also has its benefits.
