This work also demonstrates a new method for measuring the particles' affinity for surfaces by analyzing their movement over a wide range of physical forces, from stick-slip to freely rolling, while considering various factors that might influence their behavior.  This research applies to different colloidal systems, such as the movement of bacteria near surfaces with specific chemical properties, the migration of particles within cell membranes influenced by enzyme activity, or the flow of particles in solidifying fluids.  Possible implications of our findings are also discussed.

This research examines the numerical computation of the density response function in two-dimensional fractional quantum Hall systems with short-range interactions, focusing on electron density. The study reveals a multitude of collective modes, notably magnetorotons, arises from interactions, and demonstrates that the density response is regulated across all momentum states. The findings also show that interactions can be measured by modifying the energy spectrum of the spin component.

A newly proposed method for identifying and locating multiple infections within network structures is presented. This approach builds upon a previously established theorem relating to the generalized Perron-Frobenius theorem for non-negative, high-dimensional arrays and involves searching for the largest eigenvalues in specific subarrays derived from infected and uninfected node sets. A numerical efficiency comparison showed that this grouping method yields comparable outcomes to the existing message passing approach while offering significant processing speed improvements. The proposed method is demonstrated through its application to simulated and real-world data sets, showcasing its capacity to effectively and efficiently pinpoint the source of infections.

We examine the appearance of Sun's central peak, represented by the function $X(\theta,\phi)$, in the maximum probability map of the CMB at the center of a sphere with an infrared temperature of $\Delta T_{\rm IR}(\theta,\phi)$. Assuming anisotropies follow the CKPST model, we find that the central peak's amplitude peaks at $\eta_2/\sqrt{2}$ for certain values of $\eta_2$, $\eta_3$, and $\eta_4. We identify a range of these parameters where the central peak's amplitude is distinctly lower than its maximum value, resulting in a recognizable signature on the CMB's temperature multipoles. Furthermore, when the Sun's central peak appears abnormally, the central value of $\Lambda$ is significantly different from its expected value, serving as a reliable indicator of such events.

Our focus is on overcoming the challenges of goal-conditioned reinforcement learning algorithms when it comes to understanding natural language objectives that are difficult to achieve. One of the main obstacles is when the agent encounters objectives that are related to others, causing uncertainty about which goal is being referred to. To address this issue, we've proposed a new strategy called L4C, an adaptive objective framework that reinterprets the objective inputs based on the agent's current experience. By keeping a record of the goals the agent has encountered and their associated rewards, L4C dynamically adjusts the objective being pursued. Our experimental findings show that L4C enables algorithms to quickly adapt to and understand natural language objectives, as evidenced by its performance in manipulating a virtual arm to reach targets in a 3D environment.

Quantum shadow tomography is the most widely used technique for reconstructing an unknown quantum state. It has a counterpart known as shadow tomography for quantum channels, which we will be focusing on. This procedure involves using a series of quantum states to estimate how an unknown quantum channel affects certain state vectors. Although the practical implementation of this procedure can be difficult, we show that it's possible to reconstruct specific parts of the channel matrix using relatively few resources. This is particularly true if we focus on channel effects on vectors that are close to the standard basis, as this would require significantly fewer experiments. Another advantage of our method is that it enables the reconstruction of certain channel sub-matrices without prior knowledge of the channel's unitary part, which is typically obtained through quantum process tomography. This procedure is relevant for (i) quantum control systems, where controlling a small subset of the channel's effects is sufficient for good performance; and (ii) being used alongside quantum process tomography, which provides access to the channel's unitary part.

In this research, a specific class of inequalities for planar shapes with a positive Cheeger parameter is established, and established inequalities for these shapes are shown to be precise limits when the shape's Cheeger parameter tends towards zero. We provide a detailed proof of Sharp Sobolev inequality for planar shapes, and go on to prove a more general result regarding inequalities of this type that incorporate the Cheeger parameter. Additionally, this work lays groundwork for exploring inequalities in this class in even greater dimensions.

Fixed-wing Unmanned Aerial Vehicles have received considerable attention due to their extended flight duration over quasi-static conditions. Moreover, their capability to cover vast areas makes them suitable for applications such as surveillance, mapping, and data collection. Our approach focuses on an online optimization strategy for fixed-wing UAVs to maximize energy efficiency on a pre-allocated flight path within a restricted time frame. By employing a suite of available tools for fast and efficient path optimization, our results show that the quickest energy-saving method produces the best outcomes in comparison to other online techniques.

In our study, we've applied the renormalization group method to the low-energy effective model of bilayer graphene to analyze interactions between valence band edges. We've found that interactions create a resonance that reverts coupling constants to their pre-interaction state, leading to an unconventional ground state. Specifically, we've identified both ferromagnetic and valley-polarized ground states, with the latter exhibiting a unique large Fermi energy behavior similar to that of the well-studied Kekul\'e honeycomb lattice model. Notably, we've discovered that the two models share an insulating state at low energy but become unstable at next-to-leading order in Coulomb interactions, revealing a new phenomenon in which both valley and spin degrees of freedom become simultaneously aligned and then misaligned due to a resonance at $\omega \simeq \pm 2k_F$ for any small value of interaction strength. This misalignment leads to an off-equilibrium state, which may be the source of the observed long-range transport in Bernal stacked graphene.

The performance of nanomotors depends on various factors, with surface effects playing a crucial role in their functionality. The surface decoration of nanoparticles with light elements like N can influence their thermal stability. In this context, a study has been conducted to explore the surface effects on the TbN shell of Sc2TbN@C80 by analyzing it in an environment mimicking water on a flat graphene-like h-BN surface. The experimental findings reveal a shift in the magnetic pattern of the TbN layer from an irregular hexagonal arrangement to six distinct magnetic pieces as the temperature decreases. The underlying cause of this phenomenon is attributed to the distortion of the hexagonal TbN shell's conformation due to the Sc2 core's limited mobility at low temperatures. The spontaneous deformation of the TbN layer manifests as a series of irregular gaps within the magnetic pieces. In contrast, the Sc2 core's mobility at elevated temperatures enables the TbN shell to assume a uniform, gap-free hexagonal magnetic arrangement. The Sc2 core's surface effects lead to the TbN layer's conformation being sensitive to temperature, resulting in the TbN shell's gaps closing as the temperature increases. The present study confuses the concept of "gapped" and "no-gapped" structures traditionally associated with fullerenes containing atomic N. The research also introduces a novel class of nanomaterials, ScN@C80, to enable a better understanding of the temperature-dependent conformation of the TbN layer.

The internet of things encompasses diverse devices, ranging from large-scale industrial systems to tiny low-energy devices. Applications include industrial control systems, industrial automation, wearable technology, home appliances, and equipment control. The majority of IoT applications employ lightweight cryptographic algorithms due to constraints on energy consumption, processing power, and storage. This research examines current lightweight cryptographic protocols, evaluates their suitability for different IoT applications based on computational requirements, and suggests suitable algorithms based on application needs.

The Ramsey series, a widely used interleave-coding method in GPS technology, has been a key area of study for decades. Due to its historical significance, there exists a substantial body of unstructured experimental data collected through Ramseys searches conducted by various space agencies. Considering the profound impact of Ramsey measurements on cutting-edge space exploration, a proof-of-concept Bayesian approach is introduced to retrospectively optimize the design of these landmark experiments. Our comprehensive study not only applies this novel method to ancient data but also develops a cutting-edge adaptive protocol with the potential to enhance future Ramsey measurements, paving the way for enhanced sensing techniques in quantum physics and other fields.

A network's underlying structure can be its most pivotal component, 
determining not just its physical attributes but also the strategic value it holds. 
Therefore, identifying critical elements within a network, which are its most central, 
is essential for optimizing, shaping, or managing it effectively. Various measures
of a node's importance have been proposed - from simple metrics like proximity and degree 
to more complex methods like community position and behavioral influence - all aiming to 
capture a node's role within its network. While some of these methods work well for specific
purposes, they have limitations. To address this, a new approach is presented which uses a 
network's total triangle count as a fundamental importance metric. This method focuses on 
the net's ability to form triangles, which is key to its overall cohesion and structural strength 
and closely relates to the net's overall importance. This measure is easily interpretable and 
modifiable, allowing it to assess importance at multiple scales. It is also dynamic and can 
be calculated with linear complexity, making it suitable for large and complex networks. 
Furthermore, it is based on a multi-layered perspective which recognizes a node's importance 
is not only influenced by its immediate surroundings, but also by the bigger picture as well. 
This new approach is demonstrated through various real-world network examples.

The Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity is a proposed alternative to the conventional framework that effectively simulates gravitational behavior across space for static objects. Despite its simplicity, this theory has the capability to recreate a range of gravitational effects observed on Earth. Our goal in this initial paper is to establish the foundational aspects of this theory, accompanied by a validation through its ability to predict the results of specific scientific experiments. Further discussions in subsequent papers will examine the implications of this theory and its potential connections to the long-standing mystery of dark matter.

This work commences by defining operations for sets of matrix pencils under stratified equivalence and subsequently identifies the properties for these operations to form distributive lattices. Subsequently, we delve into various applications of these operations, including determining fundamental systems of cycles for matrix pencils and generating groupoids of singular matrices through pencil multiplication. Notably, we establish that the operations associated with strong stratified equivalence do, in fact, yield a distributive lattice, whereas operations associated with restricted stratified equivalence fail to satisfy this property in a consistent manner. Furthermore, we investigate other equivalence relations, namely, bundle and covering equivalences, and also explore strong stratified equivalence with respect to general matrix classes.

A novel method is formulated to compute the n-dimensional twisted torus topological T-dualized geometric classification. The technique developed relies on a precise formula that determines T-duality by comparing the magnetic vector field of the twisted torus with its electric counterpart obtained from a topological classification. The solution involves solving a set of linear equations with variable components to obtain a general expression for the electric vector field in terms of the magnetic counterpart. Subsequently, electric-magnetic duality is demonstrated for a specific example of a five-dimensional non-Abelian topological T-dual system, which involves a free particle on a five-dimensional twisted torus. The study culminates with an analysis of geometric T-duality for a specific subset of twisted tori, which exhibits symmetry in higher-dimensional manifold structures.

In the study of parametric shortest paths, a tree decomposition of a given network is used to calculate multiple values of shortest path lengths between certain points. However, this method has a limitation of exponential size, which doesn't suit networks with a small fractional treewidth. Researchers have addressed this issue by discovering an algorithm that can efficiently create a new tree decomposition with a smaller treewidth after adding an O(n log n) number of new vertices, and this new tree decomposition can then be used to calculate all pairwise shortest paths at a cost of O(n^{1/2-ε} k^O(1)) for an ε small positive value. They have also shown an algorithm can efficiently create a new tree decomposition with a treewidth of k + O(m/m') and a cost of O(m/m' + n^{1-ε'} (m/m')^{O(1)}) for an ε' a small positive value, and this new tree decomposition can be used to calculate all pairwise shortest paths between vertices in different components of the network. They have also shown the treewidth for all pairs of vertices in a network cannot be lower than a certain threshold for all pairs of vertices under a certain condition. They have also derived an algorithm that can improve on a previous method with a significant improvement in distance computation time in planar networks. They have also derived an algorithm that can improve on a previous method with a significant improvement in distance computation time in networks without a cycle. They have also derived an algorithm

For smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time dynamical systems, nearly all initial conditions lead to unique, convergent behavior, regardless of the specific details of the system's dynamics or the size of the interval. Furthermore, most of the convergent trajectories result in asymptotic convergence to a single stable fixed point or a single cycle. Additionally, most of the remaining trajectories tend towards a specific two-cycle or may diverge arbitrarily.

The potential of noise-tolerant variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies largely unexplored, yet its practical application remains uncertain due to the adverse effect of noise on both state preparation and measurement (SPIM). We investigated an alternative approach where a qubit-excitation penalty drives both circuits simultaneously, leading to a robust and efficient algorithm suitable for both intermediate- and long-term quantum simulators. Our approach outperformed the conventional VQE in finding the ground-state energy of helium-like atoms and, in comparison to a recent adaptive VQE, we saw stable results with both qubit-excitation penalty and no loss of accuracy in the intermediate results. Furthermore, we implemented a simple strategy to determine the optimal number of iterations for convergence. We tested the algorithm using both a noise-free quantum simulator and a noisy trapped ion simulator, achieving convergence in twelve iterations with the latter. We found our method converges to the exact ground-state energy, independent of the initial conditions, which was consistent with our results from the helium-like atoms example. We compared this method to the traditional VQE, which required an impractically large number of iterations. Our results indicate that noise can be mitigated by employing an adaptive qubit-excitation penalty, effectively converting what would be catastrophic errors into a usable gradient for optimization. We believe this method has the potential to enhance the performance of near-term and noisy quantum computers.

Deep generative neural networks like autoencoders and generative adversarial networks (GANs) are highly successful in representing complex data across diverse domains. A critical component of these models is the decoder, traditionally understood as a generator, which produces the output. Surprisingly, the standard formulation of these decoders is suboptimal, limited by its focus on the input-only representation, whereas in reality, many datasets benefit from both input and label information. A new type of decoder is introduced, referred to as the profound generative decoder (PGD), incorporating hidden representation and label information to optimize the encoding and decoding process. This is made possible by combining the strengths of both encoder and decoder, or more precisely, the encoder and its corresponding decoder. This integrated approach is possible due to the similarities observed between the approximate posterior representation and the combined knowledge of its decoder and gradient information. Simulations using basic datasets have demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed method.

Newly discovered cosmic phenomena during the cosmic medium's contraction may accompany an accelerated expansion. The main objective of this paper is to examine from a theoretical viewpoint two recent statements: "The accuracy of cosmology heavily relies on the precision of the Hubble constant" and "Gravitational waves from inflation may be detectable in the near future by combining signals from multiple detectors". Our analysis indicates that the scenario of cosmological contraction, triggered by watered-down inflation whose gravitational waves are amplified by loops and other mechanisms, provides a compelling background for understanding the strain on the fabric of space-time and the signals detected by LIGO-Virso and NANOGrav in the context of watered-down inflation. The stable cosmological model developed in this study is characterized by an interplay between the inflationary potential and the terms driving the cosmological contraction, leading to a coherent explanation for the discrepancy in the values of the Hubble constant as measured by different astronomical techniques and the detection of unique gravitational waves with specific properties by LIGO-Virso and NANOGrav in the near future.

Comets exhibit a range of carbon compounds, including those that form through the interaction of ices with the warm comet surface and atmosphere. Carbon monosulfide, which emits weakly at specific wavelengths, might be a significant emitter of thermal radiation in some comets, but its presence is not consistently observed. This study used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to examine Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) in the 1.3 millimeter wavelength range. The comet was observed on March 18, 2017, when it was approximately 1.3 AU away from Earth and had a temperature of 4-5 Kelvin. This is the first interferometric observation of a comet, and we presented it in the UV plane and performed an analysis to identify the thermal emission regions. The observation suggested that ER61 had a compact shape with emission regions that could be produced by water vapor and carbon monosulfide. Notably, we detected carbon monosulfide emitting over a wide range of electron depths, but not in the innermost regions, which may imply that CS originates from icy inclusions within the comet's nucleus that are activated as they move to the surface. These icy inclusions could be responsible for the variability in CS observations that have been reported in other comets.

We suggest a straightforward yet effective approach to generate speech without
training. By leveraging a comprehensive speech corpus, we develop a comprehensive
vocabulary of common syllables and phonetic sequences that are frequently used.
To create speech sounds, we design a basic syllable model that combines these
elements with probability, guided by the syllable structures observed in the
original speech data. Additionally, we generate speech through sequential addition,
starting with short syllables and gradually increasing in length, ensuring that
the generated speech stays on track with the original speech's rhythmic flow.
With a model that generates one syllable at a time, we successfully produce
creatively crafted speech outcomes that demonstrate a capacity for creativity.

Using the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, we investigate the influence of radiation/visible sector decoupling on the dark energy behavior and its interaction with a complex quintessence field. Assuming no radiation decoupling occurs, the dark energy follows a complete set of generalized equations derived from the Einstein field equation. However, with decoupling, the dark energy's behavior exhibits a change as it approaches a stable state, resulting in a fraction of dark and visible sectors' energy densities. Furthermore, a complex quintessence field is introduced to model the dark energy's dynamics, with its influence on the sector's relationship and time-dependent properties being investigated.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming issues often arise in various real-world applications, despite being notoriously difficult to solve. A novel algorithm is proposed to tackle these problems, combining the strengths of multi-objective non-linear programming approaches, multi-criteria decision-making techniques, and multi-level branch and bound methods. Specifically, the proposed algorithm incorporates non-linear programming solutions, a variant of multi-objective non-linear programming optimization, and the branch and bound utilising NSGAII approach to efficiently explore the feasible region. Through comprehensive comparisons, our proposed algorithm outperforms competing methods, including a state-of-the-art commercial software, in solving a set of demanding MOINLP test problems. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is effectively used to find Pareto-optimal solutions to a real-world VSC power flow problem, highlighting its practical utility.

We establish two key findings: Firstly, we prove that the smooth functions from a two-dimensional real interval to any Lie groupoid defined on a two-dimensional manifold have continuous sources. This means the sources of the smooth functions form a groupoid with invertible objects, aligned with the original Lie groupoid's structure. Secondly, we show that any smooth vector field along the smooth transitions within the original Lie groupoid forms a continuous source. This finding leads to the conclusion that the original Lie groupoid and its derived sources are part of a larger whole, forming a new Lie groupoid that encompasses both full and core presentations. This comprehensive finding holds true for any level of homotopy. Moreover, we identify that these two key findings inherently result from the application of the synthetic differential method, a foundational method that leads to the discovery of the maximally extensive and integrated features of smooth geometric structures. This methodology is instrumental in identifying the most comprehensive and intricate characteristics of groupoids and other smooth geometric objects below the smallest infinitesimal scale.

For biomedical informatics, the need to standardize data exchange procedures is growing rapidly.  There are numerous databases available that contain varied, high-quality datasets in various formats.  In order to streamline data access, the implementation of data portals is necessary.  These cyberinfrastructure tools, data portals, cater to diverse cyber tools that enable users to submit their data for analysis, provide data visualization, and facilitate data download.  In addition to the conventional data exchange approach, we introduce an innovative data exchange methodology that integrates data integration and data exchange.  This protocol draws upon existing standards, specifically the HL7 Clinical Document Architecture and the BioMed Ontologies' Representations of Medical Information using Ontologies.  In order to test the effectiveness of this protocol, we represent a data exchange scenario and demonstrate its application to a brain tumor dataset.  In conclusion, the developed protocol can be widely applied to various data exchange scenarios, which in turn can be easily implemented using data portals to facilitate data access.

Aspect-based emotion analysis is a critical task that requires identifying specific aspects within a text and determining the associated emotions. This approach is particularly vital for understanding detailed opinions on specific entities, as captured by sentences like "The restaurant's atmosphere was amazing but the service was unimpressive." Notably, the perspective of the reviewer significantly impacts the interpretation of the emotions. Despite the progress made so far, the sentiment hidden within hidden aspects remains unexplored. To tackle this challenge, this paper presents a novel pre-training technique called HCAP, which incorporates a distinctive contrastive loss to uncover the underlying sentiment from hidden aspects. The model's ability to capture this sentiment is achieved through a multi-view approach, with a sentence-level self-attention mechanism that enables the sharing of hidden aspects' sentiment views. As a result, this approach can leverage the shared knowledge to distinguish the expressed emotions. The proposed technique excels in its capability to uncover the hidden sentiment from hidden aspects. As evidence, it outperforms current state-of-the-art models in aspect-based sentiment analysis tasks, with notable improvements.

Researchers often study health factors by examining relationships between health factors, outcomes, and intermediate steps.  For better understanding, they use statistical models to analyze health correlations, considering how other factors may influence these connections.  Since many studies involve large groups of people, researchers use specialized sampling methods to gather data on health by comparing different groups.  In addition to these studies, researchers also use random sampling to gather data on health by focusing on people with a specific health issue and comparing them to those without it.  We have developed a statistical approach that allows researchers to find out if there is an connection between health factors, outcomes, and intermediate steps, even when data is gathered using the just mentioned methods as long as the intermediate steps affect the health issue of interest.  We have conducted an experiment to test our approach by applying it to two different health studies, one that focuses on having a specific health issue and one that compares different groups, and found that it properly identifies the connections between health factors, outcomes, and intermediate steps in both cases.

This research delves into the problems of non-interfering secure communication for multiple recipients and physical layer security enhancement in a network assisted by a reconfigurable surface, particularly in situations involving equipment capacity restrictions. The investigation comprises two main studies. Firstly, we maintain that all components of the network can maintain stable and secure connections when faced with limitations in individual equipment. In this context, we develop the first optimization problem, aiming to maximize the transmission rates of all devices while ensuring secure connections, and by doing so, we minimize the effects of equipment restrictions. The second optimization problem involves eliminating a specific vulnerability in the network, and we introduce an algorithm using the alternating maximization technique to solve these complex optimization problems. The investigation continues, and we assume that equipment restrictions do not affect the ability to maintain stable and secure connections. In this context, we define a network security level as a specific quantity and introduce a new optimization problem, aiming to maximize this level while minimizing the effects of equipment capacity constraints. The application of a specific method for solving non-convex problems allows us to obtain a solution to this optimization problem, and we introduce an alternative formulation of the equipment load to eliminate the non-convexity present in one of the terms in this equation.

The basic idea behind many modern stock picking methods seems to work in practice, yet researchers often lack clear explanations for their success. By applying decision theory principles to the analysis of resampling and rewriting techniques in data-driven stock picking strategies, this study sheds light on the underlying justifications. Notably, the examination reveals that the particular implementation of these techniques in research papers is often at odds with the methods employed in actual applications of the same techniques. By employing a backward-looking approach to analyze the outcomes of the methods, the study identifies key issues with existing implementations that skew the results. Ultimately, the investigation proposes a new evaluation framework, referred to as "hindsight summarization," to assess stock picking methods and provides code to facilitate this approach.

The solar wind's behavior near the Sun is not well understood due to a lack of detailed observations from within close proximity to the Sun.  To better understand this phenomenon, researchers are analyzing data from the Parker Solar Probe, a spacecraft that operates close to the Sun.  With its data, they are investigating the properties of the solar wind, such as its speed, temperature, and composition, specifically near an area about 27 million kilometers from the Sun.  Initially found were instances of the solar wind slowing down through a process that seems to be more significant than previously estimated.  Additionally, speed measurements indicate the presence of two distinct zones where the solar wind's speed is higher than expected to be, one near the surface and one near an area about 12,000 kilometers above the surface.  This phenomenon is not fully understood and may be related to the underlying structure of the Sun's atmosphere, specifically its outermost layer.  More research is planned to better understand these solar wind patterns and their connection to the solar breeze, a phenomenon where the solar wind's speed is affected by the Sun's atmosphere.

The action of a discrete group on a C*-algebra leads to a noncommutative countable principal bundle, with the associated total space being a noncommutative space that consists of the direct sums of the localized algebras of the group's actions, resulting in a fiber consisting of the twisted direct product of the original algebra and the group's representation algebra, with the bottom fiber being the product of the original algebra and the group's representation algebra, with the bundle having a continuous structure characterized by the actions of the group.

In this paper, we explore the cardinality of the ultrafilter space, specifically its value and range, within various frameworks of forcing. We begin by reviewing the ultrafilter space's properties, then determining the value and range in specific cases. Our investigation of the problem involves an innovative technique of reassigning the values of family of functions through a diagonalization process, first introduced by Blass and Shelah. We will also provide new insights from their work, then expand upon it by employing an additional technique known as a superalmost-disjointization process. This method allows us to create new models that can help solve the problem, while confirming an existing upper bound to the value and range from another notable paper.

We have investigated the effects of $q$-deformation on optomechanical systems with infinite-dimensional space. These systems consist of a micro-mechanical resonator and an oscillating mirror in a lossy cavity. The linear light speed in such a system is shown to be affected by the deformation parameter, leading to two possible optomechanical regimes called $q$-light and anti-$q$-light, depending on the sign of the deformation. The anti-$q$-light regime has several beneficial effects such as enhanced mechanical susceptibility, increased sensitivity in force measurements, and the ability to achieve the ground state of radiation and motion simultaneously. The lifetime of this system is significantly longer than in regular optomechanical systems in the anti-$q$-light regime.

Based on the Double-Rotors Model, which incorporates R-parity as a physical symmetry, state vectors for particles are constructed and expressed in terms of operators representing R-parity. Using a simple Hamiltonian, wave functions for particles are calculated and placed in a coordinate space framework. These wave functions are further applied to explore R-parity changing condensates and their association with particles. It's discovered in the course of this exploration that R-parity changing condensates give rise to particles that have adverse characteristics known as'scissors modes'. These adverse'scissors modes' are discussed and identified within the framework of the Double-Rotors Model.

A novel numerical approach, the Cell-mean based Neural Network (CoMe-NET), is introduced for solving both hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations. This method leverages a cell-mean operator to enhance its ability to operate on discontinuous fields, which is particularly beneficial when dealing with the issues associated with traditional neural networks that struggle with such fields. However, traditional neural networks can be modified using techniques like Local Re-Initialization (LRI) to address these limitations to some extent. By integrating elements of both methods, CoMe-NET aims to achieve superior performance across a range of non-linear partial differential equations. To validate its effectiveness, the LRI-CoMe-NET approach is empirically evaluated and compared to traditional neural networks operating under similar conditions. Results indicate that LRI-CoMe-NET can deliver significant performance enhancements of up to several orders of magnitude in a range of non-linear partial differential equations.

The upcoming ALICE experiment at the LHC will significantly enhance its detection capabilities by upgrading to the LHC's Run 3 and beyond. We will be focusing on the most critical areas for heavy-ion research, namely the collection of precise data on quark-gluon plasma characteristics such as transport coefficients and transition lines to these states. Under normal operating conditions, the experiment will collect a massive amount of center-of-mass energy amounting to 33-40 EGeV during Run 3, but by utilizing novel collision energy settings (97.5, 155, and 190 GeV) and fast data processing across multiple detectors), the experiment will be able to collect a vast amount of unique data that can aid in further study of QGP properties. In addition to these efforts, the Alice experiment is currently exploring the possibility of exceeding its design capabilities by conducting collisions at much higher center-of-mass energies (>300 GeV) in its ODD period. We will be examining the most critical factors to consider in implementing this groundbreaking concept.

We propose an innovative method to detect the temporal Unruh effect experienced by a quantum system in state $\rho$, utilizing the entanglement between future and past light cones. As time evolves, $\rho$ creates an EPR-entangled pair $\Psi_{FE}$ that is generated when the future light cone is in a Bell state $\Omega$. The entanglement rate of $\Psi_{FE}$ is represented by the time-dependent von Neumann entropy $S_{FE}(\tau) = -\text{Tr}(\tilde{\rho}_F \ln \tilde{\rho}_F)$. In systems driven by a time-dependent quantum system, $\Psi_{FE}$ and $\tilde{\rho}_F$ form closed timelike curves, leading to an accumulated Berry phase and a final entanglement phase $\Delta \phi_{FE} = 2\int_{\tau_0}^{\tau_f} \dot B \text d \tau$. This can be leveraged to develop an innovative experimental approach for detecting the temporal Unruh effect, where an arbitrary time-dependent potential is applied to a quantum system in Schrödinger evolution, potentially enabling Unruh effect detection without needing relativistic velocities.

The current timelines model relies heavily on occasion information to make accurate decisions, but implementing a timely event extraction system is a relatively understudied area in multilingual settings. In this research, we introduce the Multilingual Occasion Extraction Dataset, MEE, which contains 4,000 multilingual sentences collected from online news sources in English, German, and Turkish, as well as 9,000 detailed annotations of occasion definitions. We highlight the distinct characteristics of the dataset and its uses, presenting various extraction challenges within it. In addition, we develop and demonstrate three different timely event extraction models using classical and neural solutions, achieving an impressive F1-score of 88.21% on the entire dataset. With its unique characteristics and extensive annotations, MEE is expected to play a pivotal role in advancing research in this area, contributing significantly to future developments in multilingual NLP and multilingual TIM models.

This research investigates a fundamental issue in global vector bundle theory, specifically regarding the existence and distinctness of solutions to the push-forward equations derived from vector bundle transitions. Previous studies had addressed the existence of solutions, but raised questions about their uniqueness and the potential for differential equations to describe these transitions. Additionally, the study examines the potential application of characteristic structures to establish solutions and reveals an inherent property limiting the possibility of constructing such solutions through charactristic structures when the base space is of dimension one or two.

We studied the impact of stellar wind from a companion star on the high-energy properties and temporal variations of the black hole Cyg X-1, specifically during its "hard" spectral phase. Simulating the hard state, we examined the effects of the enhanced wind on the properties of the accretion flow and the development of "hiccups" - short, complex fluctuations in energy spectra and light patterns. These fluctuations, influenced by the enhanced wind, grow in intensity and duration when the accretion flow extends further across the disk, reaching a maximum at a specific disk radius. This critical radius corresponds to the hydrodynamic equilibrium where the most intense wind forms. Within this specific disk region, the energy generated through the mechanical and thermal conversions loses its balance and triggers the development of the "hiccups". Furthermore, we found that the enhanced wind shifts the equilibrium of the accretion flow towards larger disk radii. At the critical boundary of the innermost region, the mechanical stress from the stellar wind triggers the transfer of material towards the black hole. This specific boundary exists within the region of the disk with the highest mechanical and thermal conversions, specifically at a critical orbital radius that corresponds to a Balmer continuum emission source.

Research on non-abelian gauge theories with a term resembling aether has gained significance due to its potential research implications on non-abelian gauge theories. We evaluate the symmetries of this model, such as its non-abelian aether symmetry (NAA), which when applied to a finite temperature scenario results in an extended non-abelian aether symmetry (EAA). Additionally, this model's existence of quasi-symmetries in both its canonical and quantum mechanical forms is demonstrated. Under certain conditions, these quasi-symmetries can be recognized as genuine symmetries, leading to a corresponding number of independent EAA symmetries. Furthermore, a novel non-abelian aether transformation that conserves action at both zero and finite temperatures is formulated. We investigate the non-abelian aether transformation's implications across various parameters in a canonical context, deriving corresponding SnAAT transformations in phase space for particles and antiparticles. Moreover, this model enables us to derive the time-time component of the stress tensor within the non-abelian aether framework and to identify the class of theories encompassing both abelian and non-abelian aether theories. A thorough examination of Casimir energy is performed, illustrating that this energy is solely attributed to aether-like non-abelian gauge theory. Finally, a unified description of both abelian and non-abelian aether-like gauge theories is formulated through a effective field theory.

The diversity of writing styles, structures and content in the vast array of scientific publications makes automated analysis a daunting and resource-intensive task, typically beyond the capabilities of basic machine learning models. This paper proposes a collaborative approach, called CUSSE, in which multiple specialized networks share their expertise to rapidly train and execute high-precision, universal models. The design of CUSSE involves adapting the graph attention network to incorporate multiple module types that perform different tasks, along with a controller network that distributes the flow of data among these modules and adjusts their parameters according to content specificity and writing style. By testing CUSSE on a dataset of 7K papers from the EMNLP & NIPS conferences, we demonstrate its effectiveness in performing universal semantic analysis, universal part-of-speech identification and universal syntactic analysis.

The majority of neutron stars and black holes in binary mergers experience a burst of accretion from fallen debris, which is hot, has high oxidation, and generates intense magnetic fields. The magnetic fields and heat drive an influx of matter, enriching the neutron star with elements and influencing its cooling through nucleosynthesis and radiation emissions. Analyzing the thermal radiation from the accretion disk is a common practice in research on this topic, but it doesn't fully account for the subsequent thermal expansion of the disk and its impact on the disk's mass loss rate, which is critical for determining the exit methods of matter and subsequent events. Using the theory of magnetized rotating perfect fluid, this study calculates the stability of magnetized neutrino-cooled accretion disks with both local and global thermal expansions. Local analysis shows the disk remains stable throughout its extent, resulting in decreased mass loss rates that slowly decline, under which conditions the matter falls onto the neutron star, resulting in enhanced element enrichment and increased heat, leading to an delayed cooling. The global analysis with a specified magnetic field distribution demonstrates that the disk's mass loss rates are decreased, while the energy emitted in the infrared spectrum increases, particularly for mergers involving magnetic field strengths above 10^16 G.

Initially based on early data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam, an extremely large camera for a telescope called the Subaru, our study revisited an earlier matter concerning extremely large galaxies. These massive galaxies, known as early-type giants, grow rapidly within very distant regions of the universe. However, a previous observation of these galaxies via the Subaru, produced outcomes that contradicted expectations of a universe governed by the theories of dark matter and using a specific statistical measure of growth. To better understand these findings, our study used more data, revised a critical aspect of a galaxy's physical state, identified a significant observation within this data, and used statistical analysis to assess these results. Our study discovered that a new theory called monopole merengue merengue merengue merengue merengue merengue is capable of addressing these prior results. These theories are also used to make a prediction about an upcoming study concerning these galaxies.

This paper expands upon a previous study, the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation, to explore phenomena resulting from the ejection of charged particles. Analyzing bipolar ejections, the text demonstrates that they can serve as a repellent gravitational phenomenon and provides two potential examples, suggesting that highly charged local mass losses may be connected to the formation of comet tails and the phenomenon of galactic jets emerging from compact stars.

Radio astronomy observations have revealed fast radio bursts, extremely bright pulses of radio energy that originate from distant galaxies, with the majority occurring randomly, although some repeat. These bursts remain a mystery and their causes are still unidentified. Researchers are trying to understand the physics behind these enigmatic events by analyzing their characteristics, including the presence of additional emission that may persist after the initial burst pulse. This additional emission can provide valuable insights into the physics and surroundings of these events. However, identifying it is challenging because it requires accurate measurements of the initial burst pulse. By analyzing detailed observations of 137 pulses from 15 repeating sources and 43 single-source events, our study established limits for any ongoing or delayed emission, including its high-frequency behavior. This was done by modeling the expected emission pattern if the additional emission is due to a cloud of charged particles, which could be applied to any observed burst pulse to constrain its surroundings. This work sets tight bounds on the emission in fast radio bursts and their post-pulse behavior, particularly for the 30% of these events that have repeating sources with known distances. These findings set a firm upper limit on the emission over an extensive range of frequencies, which can be applied to any observed fast radio burst to derive its surrounding environment.

The efficiency of high-power laser production can be evaluated using the factor eta_pump→eta_saturable→eta_output, representing the ratios of pump, saturable, and output power. Increasing the pump efficiency (eta_pump) leads to lower temperature and reduced strain on the system, whereas improving the saturable threshold (eta_saturable) allows for higher beam output and lower walk-off angles. Moreover, enhancing the output efficiency (eta_output) increases overall beam power without modification to the pump or saturable thresholds. The fundamental techniques for enhancing each efficiency factor are examined, discussed, and reviewed, with analysis methods provided for implementing these strategies. The concepts of etaloning and astigmatism correction are introduced to develop specialized phases for these efficiencies, effectively manipulating the fundamental mode's propagation. The advantages of combining multiple efficiency enhancements are examined, with validation demonstrated through modeling of an axially depressed Nd:YAG laser, with accompanying design for manufacture using a commercial 808 nm laser.

The influence of pre-trained language models has significantly transformed text creation, however their full potential is still not realized when used alone. In collaboration with experts from fields including graphic design and visual storytelling, we have developed Violets, a graphical interface that enhances the capabilities of language models through the incorporation of visual elements. Unlike existing natural language processing tools, Violets enables seamless integration of images and graphics into text compositions. Through automated testing involving over 100 designers and thousands of variations, as well as expert assessment with 50 professionals, we have demonstrated that Violets successfully extends the capabilities of existing text-generating models to encompass complex visual tasks. Furthermore, we have discovered that these models are not limited by visual ability and can effectively identify and respond to complex visual concepts. Ultimately, we have found that the synergy between visual and language capabilities plays a vital role in text creation, and we believe that the innovative use of integrated Violets capabilities will revolutionize the creative process.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that incorporates Delegated Proofof-Work (DPoW), a consensus mechanism that has the added benefit of allowing miners to verify transactions without needing to fully understand the underlying spending occurrences. Our research reveals that DPoW-compatible modules, such as our RingCT protocol, have the potential to considerable speed up verification processes for module-specific data, even up to 90% faster, when compared to a pure Proof-of-Work (PoW) environment. Our proposed DPoW-RingCT system combines the security aspects of DPoW with the confidentiality aspects of RingCT, offering superior performance, all while maintaining a comparable level of complexity as standalone RingCT transactions.

In-depth analysis of the SPT-3G focus plane imaging system will rely heavily on 
brightness scans, a technique that uses moving lenses to modulate image 
intensity and reconstruct the Sun's image formation process. We are developing 
two types of brightness scans, based on either a single moving lens or two 
fixed lenses with a variable gap, respectively. We calculate the point spread 
functions for both scenarios and test their accuracy in reconstructing the Sun's 
image through simulation of real Sun conditions. We also explore how scanning 
noise impacts the measurement and discuss its effects on specific variables, 
along with proposed integration methods. We are simulating and testing the single 
scanning lens within SPT-3G's central module to determine its functionality and 
start designing the data acquisition system, using LabVIEW with a high-speed 
ADQ7-1440 GSAMP card to optimize the data acquisition process.

Our goal is to develop a predictive model that leverages both collaborative information and individual usage patterns from a recent dataset submitted to a competition, focusing on predicting 6-month cancer recurrence risks from the MUGSI6 dataset. We've been tasked with analyzing and processing the dataset, obtaining relevant collaborative information, and designing a predictive model. Through this project, we've discovered Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are well-suited for handling time-series data within the MUGSI6 dataset. However, our exploration of RNNs revealed the challenge of incorporating collaborative information and managing the inherent imbalances in the data. We've also found that certain features, including DNA methylation, exhibit systematic imbalance, necessitating further correction. Furthermore, our balance analysis suggests that developing models capable of generalizing to rare events, such as cancer recurrence, is feasible. While our model development focused on predicting the recurrence of cancer, our approach can be applied to other time-series problems within the MUGSI6 dataset, such as forecasting cancer risk over different time periods.

This research examines the sequential decays $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$. The paper presents expressions for the momentum of the lepton pair in the $\Upsilon(nS)$ frame and the diameter by square of the form factor at the pole mass of the charm quark. Studies also predict the two-body decay branching fractions of $\Upsilon(nS)$ and the mass range for the dimuon decay $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(1S)\mu^+\mu^-$. The results suggest that these decays are driven by hadronic loop processes. Assuming that np-wave contributions can be ignored, these decays are subject to CP invariance. The predicted two-body decay branching fractions for $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-,$ $\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-,$ and $\Upsilon(4S)\pi^+\pi^- ($in percentage) are $0.164,$ $0.109,$ and $0.029,$ respectively. Referring to the mass range for $\Upsilon(10753)$ considered in recent research (8.05008--8.11108 double-sided uncertainty range), the dimuon decay $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(1S)\mu^+\mu^- ($in percentage) is $0.063,$ corresponding to an expected signal

We introduce a novel optimization method, called range-sensitive stochastic gradient descent (AskewSGD), tailored for quantized neural networks. This method iteratively refines model parameters by expanding the search range for each weight and adaptively adjusts step sizes based on individual range values. AskewSGD is a highly efficient approach that ultimately converges to optimal solutions. Additionally, we developed a tool to automatically set initial search ranges and step sizes. This method requires only minor modifications to traditional stochastic gradient descent code and has minimal computational overhead. Performance results demonstrate that AskewSGD can achieve significant improvements over standard quantized training methods, leading to smaller target range sizes and higher accuracy. AskewSGD's effectiveness is showcased on various models, including MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, in combination with approaches like Label Refinery and Regularization, on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

Over the past few decades, advancements in soft robotics have led to significant breakthroughs, making robotics more capable of interacting with soft and fragile objects. A primary obstacle to fully realizing soft robotics potential lies in developing control systems that can efficiently manage these flexible bodies with minimal risk of causing damage. This paper offers an in-depth review of current methods for controlling hyperelastic structures through mathematical modeling, including the advantages and limitations of each approach. A critical examination of existing research highlights the challenges that need to be addressed for practical applications, emphasizing the need for more research in developing effective control systems for soft and hyperelastic structures. This article also identifies and links the relevant concepts to their corresponding experimental studies, paving the way for future research in soft robotics and hyperelastic control.

We revisit the Jacoby group and its subgroups, and provide new characterizations of certain subgroups and their relation to covers of the orthogonal group. Additionally, we clarify and rectify prior incorrect statements about the isomorphism of the authentic and augmented Jacoby groups, and derive a detailed algorithm for computing the authentic Jacoby group based on a given orthogonal group representation.

To establish the validity of factual information provided in tables, one effective approach is to apply fact validation, ensuring that every entry conforms to established standards. Previous methods solely focused on examining individual cells, but we've discovered that considering entire rows, each representing an entity, can provide more valuable insights into validating factual content. Our proposed model not only identifies disintegrative validation rules, allowing us to break down complex validation issues into more manageable parts, but also accurately handles multiple disintegrative rules and effectively deals with incomplete tables by filling in missing data. We have successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our approach through thorough testing on table disintegration, encompassing both English and Chinese language datasets.

Generative adversarial networks, particularly those of the 1D variational type, can generate real-looking images, however their efficiency is limited by their dimensionality. Our research focuses on a specialized variant of the 1D variational network known as the hidden space variational network (HSVN), which has seen successful application in processing the complex 32x32 images utilized in the UDA50 dataset in the field of unsupervised domain adaptation. Our paper reveals that HSVNs possess an intrinsic ability to improve the quality of the generated images by retaining and gradually rebuilding the conditional information received during training, which is derived from latent space. Conversely, using a residual connection to incorporate latent space conditionality in contrast to the hidden space results in inferior image quality and significantly hampers the network's ability to eliminate domain discrepancy. Our study further delves into the impact of learning a latent space that is informed by domain-specific information, which ultimately enables the domain discrepancy to unravel and domain similarity to emerge.

Unstructured grids, which don't follow a specific pattern, are often the most accurate type of mesh for complex geometric data. However, they can be the most expensive to compute with. A recent method to cut costs is to start with a standard grid that fits the data's boundaries, and then move to a more accurate type of grid when we need to compute more precise results. This process involves two steps: building the standard grid and refining it. In unstructured grids, there are a few methods to cut costs: always moving an entire grid section at a time, moving a part of the grid that includes new data elements, or adjusting small parts of the grid. Each of these methods has its own advantages and disadvantages. Our study is about these methods, testing them in various situations to see how well, how long they take, and how much they remember about what they've done before. To make this easier, we use a special way to group these methods in a way that's easy to work with. By grouping these methods, we see how they work together to make the process more efficient. This process is even more efficient when we use a special way to move parts of the grid that incorporates what we know about the data. A method to cut costs is even more efficient when it uses a special way to group the grid in a way that's efficient too. In the distance tagging problem, we seek an efficient way to assign a unique label to each vertex of an undirected, connected graph, where the label assigned to a vertex reflects its shortest distance to a specific reference point, and labels should be optimized for overall length. For various metric labeling problems with faults, previous research used the concept of fault lines to divide faulty regions into manageable areas. However, existing metric labeling approaches do not rely on such fault lines, and our work investigates the distance tagging problem with faults without them. To resolve this problem, we introduce the concept of pre-distance tags (PDTs), which allow us to determine the distance from a reference point to each vertex within a fault area. We propose two methods to create PDTs: randomly generated tag methods that give an approximate solution and methodically constructed tag methods that give an optimal solution. For the randomly generated tag methods, we prove its optimality by providing a upper limit for the length of the tags. For the methodically constructed tag methods, we build tags in a hierarchical fashion, starting from the root of the tree derived from the input graph and dividing it into smaller parts until each part consists of at least three vertices. For the basic methodically constructed tag methods, we provide a precise upper limit for the length of the tags, and for further optimization, we allow vertices to have the same label in their associated subgraphs, resulting in a significant improvement of the length of the tags.
